meta.blurb: In 1971 an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and they landed together. Start there and take physics one idea at a time, through energy, atoms, bent space and the puzzles nobody has solved.
meta.bible: Voice: calm, friendly and clear, speaking to You, using everyday things such as a Ball, a Kettle and a Swing; the science is real and honest about what is not yet known, with no invented numbers. Galileo: Italian scientist who argued that heavy and light things fall together once the air is gone. Isaac Newton: English scientist of the seventeenth century, laws of motion and gravity. Archimedes: ancient Greek scientist, levers and floating. Michael Faraday and James Clerk Maxwell: nineteenth century scientists of electricity and magnetism. Ernest Rutherford: showed the atom has a Nucleus. Albert Einstein: Relativity in 1905 and 1915. Werner Heisenberg: Uncertainty. Apollo: Moon missions; in 1971 an astronaut dropped a Hammer and a Feather on the Moon. CERN: laboratory near Geneva; the Higgs particle was found in 2012. Key terms: Metre, Kilometre, Newton, Friction, Gravity, Orbit, Mass, Weight, Energy, Kinetic, Potential, Entropy, Pressure, Conduction, Convection, Radiation, Frequency, Pitch, Prism, Refraction, Electron, Proton, Neutron, Nucleus, Photon, Quanta, Quantum, Quarks, Hydrogen, Helium, Fusion, Fission, Generator, Turbine, Magnetic, Electromagnetic, Galaxy, Galaxies, Celsius, Cannonball, Snowshoe, Spectacles, Telescopes, Microscopes, Hammer, Feather, Kettle, Puck, Trolley, Lever, Pulleys, Gears, Ratio, Spectrum, Stars. Facts: light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second; sound in air about 340 metres a second; the Moon's gravity is about one sixth of the Earth's; the Sun's core is about fifteen million degrees Celsius; the universe is close to fourteen billion years old; ordinary matter is about five percent of the universe. Added for the full-length book: Henry Cavendish: English scientist who measured the tiny pull between lead balls around 1798. James Watt: Scottish engineer, the Watt is named after him. Heinrich Hertz: German physicist, the Hertz is named after him. Christian Doppler: Austrian physicist, the Doppler effect. Benjamin Franklin: named positive and negative charge. Alessandro Volta: Italian scientist who made the first battery in 1800. Volta, Kilogram, Kilocalories, Amperes, Voltage, Piston, Hydraulic, Sonar, Prism, Resonance, Wavelength, Crest, Trough. More names and fixed facts: Isaac Newton: Principia 1687. Albert Michelson and Edward Morley: American scientists, 1880s, found no change in the speed of light. Urbain Le Verrier: French mathematician who calculated where Neptune must be in 1846; Johann Galle found it. Arthur Eddington: English astronomer, 1919 eclipse. John Wheeler: American physicist, spacetime phrase. Max Planck: German physicist, 1900, energy in packets. Erwin Schrodinger: Austrian physicist, cat in a box, 1935. Thomas Young: two slits, 1801. Joseph John Thomson: English physicist, found the electron in 1897. Democritus: Greek thinker, atoms. Robert Brown: pollen grains, 1827. Henri Becquerel, Marie Curie and Pierre Curie: radioactivity. Hans Christian Oersted: Danish scientist, 1820. William Herschel: found infrared in 1800. Wilhelm Rontgen: German physicist, X-rays in 1895. Paul Dirac: British physicist, antimatter. Edwin Hubble: expanding universe in the 1920s. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson: found the cosmic microwave background in 1965. Vera Rubin: American astronomer, galaxy spin. LIGO: detectors in the United States that caught gravitational waves in 2015. Event Horizon Telescope: first black hole picture in 2019, Messier 87. Large Hadron Collider: ring tunnel about 27 kilometres around near Geneva. Key terms added: Gravitational, Spacetime, Photons, Muons, Neutrinos, Antimatter, Positron, Quarks, Leptons, Radioactivity, Half-life, Transformer, Electromagnet, Aurora, Infrared, Ultraviolet, Microwave, Radio, Gamma, Doppler, Hertz, Watt, Joule. Chapters: twenty chapters of ten pages each; the last page ends the book with the ball under the first stars.
chapters: A Pull That Reaches the Moon

beats.scene: A boy throws a ball outside while a kettle steams in the kitchen
beats.summary: Physics asks simple questions about everyday things, such as a thrown ball and a hot drink.

beats.scene: A leaf and raindrops fall past a window on a grey afternoon
beats.summary: A few rules lie behind many different things, so the same idea can explain a falling leaf and a falling raindrop.

beats.scene: A girl measures a long table with a tape in a bright kitchen
beats.summary: Physics starts with careful measuring, and the metre is the shared unit for length.

beats.scene: A boy holds a stopwatch beside a runner at a school track
beats.summary: Time is measured in seconds, and a day contains 86,400 of them.

beats.scene: A woman weighs apples on a kitchen scale with a metal pan
beats.summary: Mass is the amount of matter in something and is measured in kilograms.

beats.scene: A girl drops a marble three times and checks the stopwatch each time
beats.summary: No measurement is perfect, so scientists repeat it and take an average, and they say how sure they are.

beats.scene: A cyclist, a walker and a car on a country road
beats.summary: Speed is the distance something travels divided by the time it takes.

beats.scene: A cyclist climbs a steep hill and then races down the far side
beats.summary: An average speed hides the changes along a journey; the speed at one instant is what the speedometer shows.

beats.scene: Two walkers pass each other on a long straight path in opposite directions
beats.summary: Velocity is speed together with direction, so two walkers with the same speed can have different velocities.

beats.scene: A hand draws a line on graph paper beside a toy car
beats.summary: A graph of distance against time shows motion at a glance: a steep line means fast, a flat line means stopped.

beats.scene: A passenger is pressed back into a car seat as the car pulls away
beats.summary: Acceleration is a change in speed or direction, and we feel it in our bodies.

beats.scene: Passengers lurch forward on a bus as it stops at a busy stop
beats.summary: Slowing down is a kind of acceleration too, pointing the opposite way, and it throws us forward.

beats.scene: A bus turns a corner while a woman holds a rail and leans sideways
beats.summary: Because velocity includes direction, turning at a steady speed is acceleration too.

beats.scene: A man in a glass lift feels heavy as it starts to rise
beats.summary: In a lift that starts upward you feel a little heavier, and when it stops you feel a little lighter.

beats.scene: A stone drops from a bridge, with a dotted trail showing it gaining speed
beats.summary: A falling object speeds up steadily, gaining about ten metres a second of speed every second.

beats.scene: An old scholar in a robe watches two stones fall
beats.summary: For centuries people believed heavy things fall faster, until Galileo argued that they do not.

beats.scene: A wooden ramp with a small ball rolling down and a row of marks
beats.summary: Galileo slowed the fall down by rolling balls down ramps, so that he could time them and see them speed up steadily.

beats.scene: A feather and a coin fall beside crumpled and flat paper
beats.summary: In air a feather falls slower than a coin because air pushes against it, and a crumpled paper falls faster than a flat one.

beats.scene: An astronaut drops a hammer and a feather on the grey Moon
beats.summary: Without air, heavy and light things fall at the same rate, as Galileo reasoned and a Moon experiment showed.

beats.scene: A skydiver falls through the clouds, and then a parachute opens above her
beats.summary: In air a falling person stops speeding up when the push of the air equals the pull of the Earth, and a parachute makes that top speed much smaller.

beats.scene: A young man writes by candlelight at a desk piled with books
beats.summary: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, set out three rules of motion in a famous book published in 1687.

beats.scene: A puck slides across a smooth frozen lake with nobody near it
beats.summary: Newton's first law: a moving object keeps going in a straight line at the same speed unless a force acts on it.

beats.scene: A coin on a card over a glass, and a flicking finger
beats.summary: Inertia is the tendency of things to keep doing what they are already doing, which is why a coin drops into a glass when the card is flicked away.

beats.scene: A crash-test dummy wears a seat belt as a car stops
beats.summary: In a sudden stop your body keeps moving forward, which is why a seat belt is needed.

beats.scene: A girl pushes an empty trolley, then a full one, across a shop floor
beats.summary: Newton's second law: a bigger force gives more acceleration, and more mass gives less.

beats.scene: A spring scale pulls a toy cart along a table
beats.summary: Doubling the force doubles the acceleration, and doubling the mass halves it; the unit of force is the newton, about the weight of a small apple.

beats.scene: A swimmer pushes the water backwards with her hands and glides forwards
beats.summary: Newton's third law: forces come in pairs, and a push is always matched by an equal push back.

beats.scene: A rocket lifts off above a column of fire and gas
beats.summary: A rocket pushes hot gas down and is pushed up in return, and it works in empty space because it needs nothing to push against but its own gas.

beats.scene: Footprints in wet sand beside a person slipping on a patch of smooth ice
beats.summary: When you walk you push the ground backwards and the ground pushes you forwards; on ice the push is weak and you slip.

beats.scene: A boy on roller skates pushes against a wall and rolls away backwards
beats.summary: The two forces of a pair act on different objects, so they do not cancel; the boy pushes the wall and the wall pushes the boy.

beats.scene: A boy slides a box across a rough floor until it stops
beats.summary: Friction is the rubbing force that slows moving things on Earth, and it is why a pushed box stops.

beats.scene: A runner's shoe grips a wet path beside a car with its brakes on
beats.summary: Friction is useful: it lets us walk, grip, write and brake, and without it nothing would stay put.

beats.scene: A boy rubs his hands together while smoke rises from two rubbed sticks
beats.summary: Friction turns the energy of motion into heat, which is why rubbing your hands warms them.

beats.scene: A man sits under an apple tree while the pale Moon rises behind it
beats.summary: Newton realised that the force that pulls an apple down also holds the Moon, and every object pulls on every other.

beats.scene: Two apples and two huge planets, each one pulled towards the other by arrows
beats.summary: Gravity is a pull between every pair of objects, stronger for bigger masses and weaker as the distance grows.

beats.scene: A scientist watches small lead balls hang near two large ones
beats.summary: The pull between everyday objects is far too small to feel, but the English scientist Henry Cavendish measured it around 1798.

beats.scene: A cannon on a mountain fires a ball that curves around a small Earth
beats.summary: An orbit is a fall that never reaches the ground, because the object keeps missing the planet.

beats.scene: An astronaut floats inside a space station while the blue Earth glides below
beats.summary: A space station about 400 kilometres up orbits every 90 minutes, and everything in it falls together, so it seems weightless.

beats.scene: A girl on the Moon holds a bag of apples that feels light
beats.summary: Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same; weight is the pull of gravity and changes with the place.

beats.scene: The Moon over a calm sea at the turn of a high tide
beats.summary: The Moon's pull makes the oceans bulge, and as the Earth turns most coasts see about two high tides a day.

beats.scene: A sunlit kitchen with a boiling pot, a bicycle and a lit lamp
beats.summary: Energy is the ability to make change happen, and it comes in many forms.

beats.scene: A heavy truck and a small car drive side by side along a motorway
beats.summary: Moving things carry kinetic energy, which grows with mass and grows much faster with speed: double the speed, four times the energy.

beats.scene: A heavy book on a high shelf above a girl standing on a chair
beats.summary: Raising an object stores energy in it, called potential energy, which can be turned into motion if the object is allowed to fall.

beats.scene: A child on a swing at the highest point of its arc
beats.summary: On a swing, stored energy of height and energy of motion keep changing places.

beats.scene: A roller coaster train at the top of a hill above a valley
beats.summary: Energy is never created or destroyed; it changes form, and some always spreads out as heat.

beats.scene: A man carries a heavy bag up a staircase
beats.summary: Work in physics means moving something with a force, and it is a way of transferring energy.

beats.scene: Two lamps, one dim and one bright, beside a small and a large engine
beats.summary: Power is how fast energy is used or moved, and it is measured in watts.

beats.scene: A runner eats a banana beside a table of bread, rice and fruit
beats.summary: Food stores chemical energy that our bodies release; many adults use roughly 2,000 kilocalories a day.

beats.scene: A campfire burns beside a battery and a tank of petrol
beats.summary: Wood, petrol and batteries all store chemical energy that is released when they react.

beats.scene: A rubber ball bounces lower and lower on a hard floor
beats.summary: Every bounce loses a little energy as heat and sound, so the ball bounces lower and finally stops, though the total energy is not lost.

beats.scene: A boy lifts a heavy stone using a long plank resting on a log
beats.summary: A lever trades a small push over a long distance for a big push over a short one, and saves no energy.

beats.scene: An old Greek scholar stands beside a long wooden lever and a boat
beats.summary: Archimedes, an ancient Greek scientist, explained the lever and is said to have boasted that he could move the world with a long enough one.

beats.scene: A heavy child near the middle of a seesaw, a light one far out
beats.summary: A seesaw balances when a heavy load close to the middle is matched by a light load far from it.

beats.scene: A rope runs over a wheel above a well and bucket
beats.summary: A pulley changes the direction of a pull, and a system of pulleys can cut the force needed in exchange for pulling more rope.

beats.scene: A worker pushes a heavy barrel up a long ramp onto a lorry
beats.summary: A ramp lets you raise a load with a smaller force by pushing it over a longer distance.

beats.scene: An axe splits a log beside a jar with a screw-on lid
beats.summary: A wedge turns a push forward into a push sideways, and a screw is a ramp wrapped around a rod.

beats.scene: Two toothed gear wheels of different sizes turn together inside a clock
beats.summary: Gears pass motion from wheel to wheel, and a small gear turning a big one trades speed for turning force.

beats.scene: A screwdriver with a thick handle turns a screw into a wooden board
beats.summary: A wheel and axle is a lever that goes round and round: a fat handle turning a thin shaft gives extra turning force.

beats.scene: A cyclist rides uphill, with the chain and gears in clear view
beats.summary: A bicycle combines levers, wheels and gears, and low gears let a rider climb a hill with less push but more pedalling.

beats.scene: Two people do equal work, one using a ramp, one lifting straight
beats.summary: No machine saves energy: what is gained in force is paid for in distance, and some energy is always lost to friction.

beats.scene: A knife cutting bread beside a boot in snow and a wide snowshoe
beats.summary: Pressure is force divided by area, which is why a sharp knife cuts and a snowshoe stays on top of snow.

beats.scene: A diver descends in clear blue water beside a thick dam wall
beats.summary: Pressure in water grows with depth, which is why dams are thicker at the bottom and divers feel it in their ears.

beats.scene: A car rises on a garage lift beside a small pump handle
beats.summary: Pressure in a liquid is passed on equally in every direction, so a small push on a small piston can lift a heavy car on a big one.

beats.scene: An old Greek scholar sits in a bath as water spills over its rim
beats.summary: A famous story says Archimedes noticed the water rising in his bath and saw how to measure an object's volume by the water it pushes aside.

beats.scene: A huge steel ship floats in a harbour beside a stone sinking in water
beats.summary: A floating object pushes water aside and is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of that water.

beats.scene: A ship's hull full of air beside a solid steel block
beats.summary: A ship floats because its hollow hull holds a lot of air, so the whole ship is lighter than the water it pushes aside.

beats.scene: A submarine rises towards the surface from a dark blue sea
beats.summary: A submarine sinks by letting water into its tanks and rises by pushing the water out with air.

beats.scene: A girl holds a book while a thin layer of air wraps the Earth
beats.summary: Air has weight, and the air above us presses with about one kilogram on every square centimetre at sea level; higher up there is less air above, so less pressure.

beats.scene: A girl sips juice through a straw on a hilltop under a thin cloud
beats.summary: Drinking through a straw does not pull juice up: lowering the pressure in the straw lets the air pressing on the juice push it up.

beats.scene: A red hot-air balloon rises over green hills beside a tethered blue balloon
beats.summary: A balloon filled with hot air floats up because it is lighter than the cooler air it pushes aside, just as a ship floats on water.

beats.scene: A steaming mug of tea beside a mug of cold water
beats.summary: Temperature measures how fast the tiny particles in a material are moving on average.

beats.scene: A thermometer in boiling water beside a thermometer in melting ice
beats.summary: On the Celsius scale water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees at sea level.

beats.scene: A cold laboratory with frost on a metal tube and a blue glowing gas
beats.summary: There is a lowest possible temperature, absolute zero, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, where particles have almost no motion left.

beats.scene: An ice cube, a pan of water and rising steam on a stove
beats.summary: Solid, liquid and gas are the same particles with different amounts of energy.

beats.scene: A pan of ice and water on a hotplate with a thermometer reading zero
beats.summary: Melting and boiling take in a lot of energy, so melting ice stays at zero degrees until all of it has melted.

beats.scene: A puddle shrinks in the sun beside a girl wiping sweat from her face
beats.summary: Evaporation lets the fastest particles escape from a liquid, which cools what is left, and that is how sweat cools us.

beats.scene: A railway track with a small gap between two steel rails
beats.summary: Most materials expand when heated, so bridges and tracks need small gaps, and in cold weather they shrink again.

beats.scene: A metal spoon warms in hot soup beside a wooden spoon that stays cool
beats.summary: Conduction is heat moving through a material from particle to particle, and metals conduct heat much better than wood or plastic.

beats.scene: Warm air rises above a radiator in a room, with arrows showing a loop
beats.summary: Convection is heat carried by a moving fluid: warm air or water rises, cooler fluid sinks, and a circulation starts.

beats.scene: A girl warms her hands before a campfire under a clear evening sky
beats.summary: Radiation is heat carried by light and other waves, and it needs no material at all, which is how the Sun warms the Earth across empty space.

beats.scene: A woolly jumper, a flask and a double-glazed window in a cold house
beats.summary: Insulators such as wool, trapped air and a vacuum flask slow the flow of heat.

beats.scene: A cup of coffee cooling on a table as its steam fades
beats.summary: Heat flows by itself from hot to cold and never the other way, until both have the same temperature.

beats.scene: Hot water poured into a bowl of cold water, with swirling colours
beats.summary: When hot and cold water mix, the result is warm, and it does not separate again by itself, because the mixed state is overwhelmingly more likely.

beats.scene: A tidy stack of cards beside a shuffled heap spread across a table
beats.summary: Entropy measures how spread out energy is, or how many ways a situation can happen; it tends to increase.

beats.scene: An old steam engine pulls a train through a cloud of steam
beats.summary: A steam engine turns heat into motion: hot steam pushes a piston, and the invention powered the Industrial Revolution.

beats.scene: A car engine with a bright glow and heat waves rising from the bonnet
beats.summary: No engine can turn all heat into work: some must always flow to a colder place, so a car wastes much of its fuel energy as heat.

beats.scene: An inventor stares at a wheel with weights fixed around its rim
beats.summary: A perpetual motion machine, which would run for ever without an energy supply, is impossible, because energy is conserved and some always spreads out.

beats.scene: A kitchen refrigerator with its door open and warm air rising from its back
beats.summary: A fridge pumps heat from the cold inside to the warm room using electricity, so heat can be made to flow uphill, at a cost.

beats.scene: A broken egg on a floor beside a whole egg on a shelf
beats.summary: Entropy gives time a direction: an egg breaks but never mends, because the scattered state is far more likely.

beats.scene: The Sun shines above green plants, a river and clouds over a hillside
beats.summary: The Earth is not a closed system: sunlight brings in energy that powers life and weather, and the Earth radiates heat back to space.

beats.scene: Ripples spread across a pond from a pebble, with a leaf floating nearby
beats.summary: A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the material it moves through.

beats.scene: A wavy line with crests and troughs and a gap marked between two crests
beats.summary: A wave has crests and troughs; the wavelength is the gap between crests, and the frequency is how many pass each second, measured in hertz.

beats.scene: A long spring toy stretched along a floor with a ripple running down it
beats.summary: Waves can shake sideways, like a rope, or push and pull along their path, like a stretched spring.

beats.scene: A girl plucks a guitar string while a boy rests a hand on it
beats.summary: Sound is a vibration that travels through air as a wave of squeezes and stretches.

beats.scene: A bell rings inside a glass jar connected to a pump
beats.summary: Sound needs something to travel through; in a famous experiment a bell fades as air is pumped out of its jar, and in space there is no sound.

beats.scene: A flash of lightning over a hill and a girl counting on her fingers
beats.summary: Sound travels at about 340 metres a second in air, much slower than light, which is why thunder comes after lightning.

beats.scene: A short thin string and a long thick string beside a large drum
beats.summary: Pitch depends on how fast a sound vibrates, and loudness on how much energy the wave carries.

beats.scene: A man shouts across a valley towards a steep cliff on the far side
beats.summary: Sound bounces off hard surfaces as an echo, and bats and ships use echoes to find their way and to map the sea floor.

beats.scene: An ambulance with flashing lights drives past a woman at the roadside
beats.summary: The Doppler effect: a moving source squeezes its waves ahead and stretches them behind, so a siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it leaves.

beats.scene: A child on a swing being pushed at just the right moment each time
beats.summary: Resonance is a big response to pushes that match an object's natural rhythm, as with a swing or a singer's note shaking a glass.

beats.scene: Sunlight streams through a window across a dusty room
beats.summary: Light is extremely fast, about 300,000 kilometres a second, and reaches us from the Sun in a little over eight minutes.

beats.scene: A tall tree casts a long shadow across a lawn beside a sundial
beats.summary: Light travels in straight lines, which is why shadows have sharp shapes and why sundials can tell the time.

beats.scene: A bright star over a dark mountain, with a long beam of light
beats.summary: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about nine and a half million million kilometres, and starlight is old when it reaches us.

beats.scene: A girl looks at her reflection in a mirror
beats.summary: A mirror reflects light so that the angle it arrives at equals the angle it leaves at, which is why a smooth surface gives a clear image.

beats.scene: A glass prism splits a beam of white light into a band of colours
beats.summary: Newton showed that a prism splits white light into a spectrum of colours and that a second prism can join them back, so white light is a mixture.

beats.scene: A rainbow arches over a green hillside after a shower
beats.summary: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters raindrops, reflects inside and leaves bent, with each colour bent by a slightly different amount.

beats.scene: A red apple, a green leaf and a black cat sit in the sunlight
beats.summary: An object looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs the other colours; black things absorb almost all light.

beats.scene: A spoon looks bent in a glass of water beside a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Light bends when it passes between materials, which is refraction, and curved glass makes lenses.

beats.scene: A girl in spectacles reads a book beside a large lens
beats.summary: A curved lens bends light to a focus; spectacles and the lens of the eye work this way, and the eye forms an image on the retina at the back.

beats.scene: An astronomer with a long telescope beside a scientist with a microscope
beats.summary: Telescopes and microscopes are lenses that show the very far and the very small; Galileo saw moons around Jupiter in 1610.

beats.scene: A girl rubs a balloon on her hair and the hair lifts
beats.summary: Matter carries positive and negative charge; opposite charges attract and like charges repel.

beats.scene: Two pairs of charged balls, one pair pulling and one pair pushing
beats.summary: There are two kinds of charge, called positive and negative; unlike charges attract and like charges repel.

beats.scene: Lightning strikes near a house with a metal rod on its roof
beats.summary: Lightning is a huge electric spark between clouds and the ground, and a lightning rod gives it a safe path.

beats.scene: A copper wire with a plastic coating beside a hand holding a plug
beats.summary: Metals are conductors because some electrons are free to move; plastic and rubber are insulators because their electrons stay put.

beats.scene: A pile of metal discs and cloth on a table in an old laboratory
beats.summary: In 1800 the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta made the first battery, a pile of metal discs, which gave a steady current for the first time.

beats.scene: A battery, a wire and a small bulb glowing on a table
beats.summary: An electric current is a flow of charge around a closed loop, pushed by a battery.

beats.scene: Two water tanks joined by a pipe, one high and one low
beats.summary: Voltage is the push that drives a current, like the height difference that drives water, while the current is how much charge flows each second, measured in amperes.

beats.scene: A thin glowing filament inside a light bulb beside a toaster with red wires
beats.summary: Resistance is how much a material opposes a current; a thin wire resists strongly, so it heats up and glows, as in a bulb or a toaster.

beats.scene: A string of small lights on a tree, with one bulb dark
beats.summary: In a series circuit one break stops everything, while in a parallel circuit each branch works alone, which is how houses are wired.

beats.scene: A fuse in a plug beside a switch panel on a wall
beats.summary: A fuse or circuit breaker cuts off a current that grows too large, and mains electricity is dangerous and must be treated with great care.

beats.scene: A small iron nail jumps towards a dark stone magnet on a wooden table
beats.summary: Magnets attract iron; every magnet has two poles, north and south, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract.

beats.scene: Iron filings form curved lines around a bar magnet on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: A magnet fills the space around it with a magnetic field, and iron filings line up along the curved field lines.

beats.scene: A compass needle points north above a map and a small magnet
beats.summary: A compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with the Earth's field, so the Earth acts as a giant magnet.

beats.scene: Green and purple lights ripple across a dark sky above a snowy field
beats.summary: Charged particles from the Sun are steered by the Earth's field towards the poles, where they make the glowing aurora.

beats.scene: A compass needle swings beside a wire connected to a battery
beats.summary: In 1820 the Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted saw a compass needle move near a wire carrying a current, showing that electricity makes magnetism.

beats.scene: A crane with a huge round magnet lifts scrap metal in a yard
beats.summary: An electromagnet is a coil of wire around iron that becomes a magnet when current flows, and it can be switched on and off.

beats.scene: A small electric motor turns a fan beside a battery
beats.summary: A motor uses the force of a magnet on a current-carrying coil to make it spin, and it turns electrical energy into motion.

beats.scene: A scientist moves a magnet in and out of a coil
beats.summary: In 1831 Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet near a coil of wire makes an electric current.

beats.scene: A wind turbine turns above fields beside power lines
beats.summary: A generator turns a magnet inside coils to make current; wind, water or steam turns it, and generators produce most of our electricity.

beats.scene: Tall pylons carry power lines over hills towards a distant town at dusk
beats.summary: A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current, and power lines use very high voltage to lose less energy on long journeys.

beats.scene: A Scottish scientist writes equations on a blackboard in a plain study
beats.summary: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell joined electricity and magnetism in one theory, which predicted waves travelling at the speed of light.

beats.scene: A man in a workshop holds a loop of wire beside a spark
beats.summary: In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made radio waves in a laboratory and showed that they behave like light, which proved Maxwell right.

beats.scene: A radio tower, a microwave oven and a sunny window side by side
beats.summary: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and radio, microwaves and X-rays are the same kind of wave with other lengths.

beats.scene: A phone, a radio and a television aerial under a sky of invisible signals
beats.summary: Radio waves are the longest of the family and carry sound, pictures and data to radios, televisions, phones and wireless networks.

beats.scene: A kitchen microwave oven glows while a bowl of soup turns slowly inside
beats.summary: A microwave oven uses short radio waves that shake the water molecules in food, which warms it from the inside.

beats.scene: A snake and a warm cup glow orange in a dark camera view
beats.summary: Infrared is the heat radiation given off by anything warm; the astronomer William Herschel found it in 1800, and special cameras see it in the dark.

beats.scene: A narrow rainbow band marked between a long radio wave and a tiny X-ray
beats.summary: Visible light is the small band of wavelengths our eyes detect, from about 700 down to 400 billionths of a metre, and the Sun gives out most of its energy there.

beats.scene: A girl in a sun hat puts on sun cream on a bright beach
beats.summary: Ultraviolet light, shorter than violet, comes from the Sun and can burn skin; the ozone layer blocks most of the harmful part, and bees can see it.

beats.scene: A doctor holds a grey X-ray of a hand to the light
beats.summary: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are stopped by bone, so they show the inside of the body; Wilhelm Röntgen discovered them in 1895.

beats.scene: A bright burst of invisible rays leaves a distant exploding star in deep space
beats.summary: Gamma rays are the shortest and most energetic waves, made by radioactive nuclei and by violent events in space, and they are used to sterilise equipment and to treat cancer.

beats.scene: A single human hair on a table beside a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Everything is made of atoms, so small that hundreds of thousands of them fit side by side across the width of a hair.

beats.scene: An ancient Greek thinker holds a stone and looks at a pile of sand
beats.summary: The ancient Greek thinker Democritus suggested that matter is made of tiny uncuttable pieces called atoms, but he had no way of testing the idea.

beats.scene: Specks of pollen jiggle in a drop of water under a microscope
beats.summary: Pollen grains in water jiggle at random; in 1905 Einstein explained this as water molecules bumping them, which persuaded doubters that atoms are real.

beats.scene: A shelf of jars holding different metals, gases and powders in a laboratory
beats.summary: There are about ninety kinds of atom in nature, called elements, from hydrogen the lightest to uranium the heaviest, and each is its own substance.

beats.scene: A glowing glass tube with a beam of light bending beside a magnet
beats.summary: In 1897 Joseph John Thomson found the electron, a particle far lighter than any atom, which showed that atoms have parts.

beats.scene: A faint cloud of dots surrounds a tiny bright core in the middle
beats.summary: Rutherford fired particles at gold foil around 1909 and found that a few bounced straight back, which showed that an atom has a tiny dense nucleus.

beats.scene: A pea in the middle of a vast stadium, with tiny specks around
beats.summary: An atom is mostly empty space: if the nucleus were a pea in the middle of a stadium, the electrons would be tiny specks at the outer seats.

beats.scene: Two small hydrogen atoms and one larger oxygen atom join into a water molecule
beats.summary: Electrons decide how atoms join: atoms share or swap them to form molecules, such as water, which has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

beats.scene: A scientist holds a small glowing rock beside a device that clicks
beats.summary: Some nuclei are unstable and break up by themselves, giving off energy, which is radioactivity; its rate is described by a half-life, the time for half of the atoms to change.

beats.scene: The Sun shines above a calm sea beside a nuclear power station
beats.summary: The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium, while power stations on Earth split heavy nuclei in fission; both release energy from the nucleus.

beats.scene: A beam of light races ahead of a runner on a long straight road
beats.summary: Maxwell's theory gave one fixed speed for light, which puzzled physicists, and careful experiments in the 1880s found no sign of any difference with the Earth's motion.

beats.scene: A young clerk writes at a desk in a busy patent office in Bern
beats.summary: In 1905 Albert Einstein, working as a patent clerk in Switzerland, published several papers that changed physics, including special relativity.

beats.scene: A cyclist chases a beam of light that races ahead
beats.summary: Einstein took the puzzle at its word: everyone measures the same speed for light, however fast they themselves are moving.

beats.scene: A silver train rushes past a station platform with a clock on the wall
beats.summary: Special relativity: everyone measures the same speed for light, and moving clocks tick more slowly.

beats.scene: A beam of light bounces between two mirrors inside a moving carriage
beats.summary: A light clock bounces light between two mirrors; for a moving clock the light must travel a longer slanted path at the same speed, so each tick takes longer.

beats.scene: An airliner carries a small clock above a clock that stays on the ground
beats.summary: Experiments agree with relativity: atomic clocks flown in aircraft in 1971 ran slightly differently from clocks on the ground, and fast particles from the sky live longer.

beats.scene: A rocket speeds up in deep space beside a bright beam
beats.summary: Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light, because the faster something goes, the more energy is needed for each extra bit of speed.

beats.scene: Two lightning flashes strike either end of a train
beats.summary: Events that seem simultaneous to one observer can happen at different times for another, so there is no universal now.

beats.scene: A small pebble on a table with a bright beam of light above it
beats.summary: Mass is a form of energy, so a tiny amount of mass equals a huge amount of energy.

beats.scene: The Sun glows in a black sky above a scale showing a falling weight
beats.summary: The Sun turns about four million tonnes of its mass into light every second, which is how mass-energy shows up in nature.

beats.scene: Einstein stands at a blackboard with a falling apple sketched beside equations
beats.summary: Special relativity did not fit Newton's gravity, so Einstein spent about ten years searching for a new theory of gravity, finished in 1915.

beats.scene: A man floats inside a falling lift beside a hanging ball
beats.summary: Einstein's happiest thought: a person falling freely feels no weight, so gravity and acceleration are closely linked.

beats.scene: A heavy ball sinks into a stretched sheet while a marble curves around it
beats.summary: General relativity: gravity is the bending of space and time, and planets follow the curved paths.

beats.scene: A grid of lines drawn on a sheet bends around a round weight
beats.summary: Space and time are joined into one four-part thing called spacetime, and matter tells it how to curve while it tells matter how to move.

beats.scene: A dark disc covers the Sun while stars shine in the sky
beats.summary: In 1919 Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the Sun during an eclipse and found their light was bent as Einstein predicted, which made Einstein famous.

beats.scene: A tall tower with one clock at the top and one at the bottom
beats.summary: Time runs slightly slower where gravity is stronger, so a clock at the bottom of a tower ticks more slowly than one at the top.

beats.scene: A satellite orbits the Earth above a phone showing a map
beats.summary: GPS satellites carry clocks that must be corrected for relativity, or position errors would grow by kilometres every day.

beats.scene: A dark round shadow ringed by glowing gas in a starry sky
beats.summary: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

beats.scene: A ring of glowing orange light surrounds a dark centre in space
beats.summary: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first picture of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87, and later one in our own galaxy.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together in space with ripples spreading out
beats.summary: In 2015 the LIGO detectors caught gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime from two black holes that merged over a billion years ago.

beats.scene: A metal poker glows from dull red to bright white-yellow in a furnace
beats.summary: Hot things glow with a colour set by temperature, which classical physics could not explain until Max Planck in 1900 suggested energy comes in small packets.

beats.scene: Light shines on a clean metal plate while tiny sparks fly from its surface
beats.summary: In 1905 Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by saying light comes in packets called photons, and each one can knock out one electron.

beats.scene: A neon sign glows beside a band of coloured lines
beats.summary: Electrons in atoms can have only certain energies, so each element gives out light of only certain colours; this lets astronomers find what stars are made of.

beats.scene: A ball rolls down a smooth slope beside a staircase of single steps
beats.summary: Quantum theory began with the discovery that energy comes in separate packets, and light arrives as photons.

beats.scene: A beam of light passes through two narrow slits onto a striped screen
beats.summary: In the double-slit experiment light through two slits makes bright and dark stripes, as waves from the two slits add and cancel.

beats.scene: Single dots build up into a striped pattern on a screen behind two slits
beats.summary: Even single electrons sent one at a time through two slits slowly build up the stripe pattern, so each seems to act as both a particle and a wave.

beats.scene: A blurred running dog beside a sharp, still one
beats.summary: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle of 1927 says that a particle's position and motion cannot both be known exactly, and it is a rule of nature and not a problem with instruments.

beats.scene: A foggy night sky with a faint blurred dot of light in the middle
beats.summary: Quantum theory predicts chances rather than certainties, and the exact meaning of those chances is still debated.

beats.scene: A cat sits beside a sealed box in a quiet laboratory
beats.summary: Erwin Schrödinger's cat was a thought experiment from 1935 meant to show how strange it sounds to apply quantum rules to everyday things; physicists still disagree about what happens when we measure.

beats.scene: A laser beam, a computer chip and a hospital scanner side by side
beats.summary: Quantum physics underlies lasers, transistors and computer chips, medical scanners and atomic clocks, and quantum computers are being developed.

beats.scene: A huge circular tunnel under farmland beside a giant glowing detector
beats.summary: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks, which were found by smashing particles together in huge machines such as the Large Hadron Collider near Geneva.

beats.scene: A chart of small coloured squares, each labelled with a particle, on a wall
beats.summary: The Standard Model lists the basic particles: six quarks, six lighter particles including the electron, and the particles that carry the forces.

beats.scene: Four arrows labelled gravity, electric, strong and weak pull on a tiny atom
beats.summary: Nature has four basic forces: gravity, electromagnetism, the strong force that holds nuclei together and the weak force behind some radioactive decay.

beats.scene: A glowing trail of tracks inside a detector marks a rare particle collision
beats.summary: In 2012 scientists at CERN announced the Higgs particle, a sign of a field that gives mass to other particles, which had been predicted in 1964.

beats.scene: A bright flash where a glowing particle meets its mirror twin inside a scanner
beats.summary: Antimatter particles are mirror twins of ordinary ones; when the two meet they turn into energy, and PET scanners in hospitals use this.

beats.scene: Hundreds of galaxies glow in dark space seen through a big telescope
beats.summary: Our Sun is one star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is one of hundreds of billions of galaxies.

beats.scene: A line of tiny galaxies drawing away from a central watcher
beats.summary: In the 1920s astronomers including Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies are moving apart, because space itself is stretching.

beats.scene: A dim glow of ancient light fills a dark speckled sky
beats.summary: The universe began hot and dense close to fourteen billion years ago, and its faint afterglow, the cosmic microwave background, was found in 1965.

beats.scene: A spinning spiral galaxy glows in a dark sky with a faint haze
beats.summary: Galaxies spin faster than their visible matter can explain, so scientists think an unseen dark matter holds them together; it has never been directly detected.

beats.scene: Bars of different heights, with a small slice for ordinary matter
beats.summary: Ordinary matter is only about five percent of the universe; about a quarter is dark matter, and the rest is a dark energy that is speeding up the expansion.

beats.scene: A scientist writes results in a notebook beside a laboratory experiment
beats.summary: Physics works by testing: a theory must predict something an experiment could disprove, and good theories survive many tests.

beats.scene: An astronomer points a telescope at a small blue planet in a dark sky
beats.summary: In 1846 Urbain Le Verrier calculated from Newton's laws where an unseen planet must be pulling on Uranus, and astronomers found Neptune within a degree of the spot.

beats.scene: The tiny planet Mercury circles close to the bright Sun with a drawn orbit
beats.summary: Mercury's orbit drifts slightly in a way Newton's gravity could not explain; a hidden planet was proposed but never found, and general relativity explained it in 1915.

beats.scene: A cable runs behind a computer in a laboratory beside a loose plug
beats.summary: In 2011 an experiment in Italy seemed to show particles faster than light, but the cause was a loose cable, and the result went away once it was fixed.

beats.scene: Scientists in two different laboratories compare the same measurement on screens
beats.summary: A discovery counts only when independent teams repeat it and the evidence is strong enough that chance is very unlikely to explain it.

beats.scene: Two puzzle pieces, one tiny and one huge, that do not fit together
beats.summary: General relativity and quantum theory both work well but do not yet fit into one theory of gravity.

beats.scene: A blackboard covered with tiny loops, strings and many question marks
beats.summary: Ideas such as string theory and loop quantum gravity try to unite gravity and quantum theory, but none has yet been confirmed by an experiment.

beats.scene: A night sky with a few big question marks hanging above a quiet observatory
beats.summary: Open questions include what dark matter and dark energy are, why matter outweighs antimatter and what happened at the very start of the universe.

beats.scene: A kitchen with a kettle, a phone, a fridge and a sunny window
beats.summary: The ideas of the book are at work in an ordinary day: Newton's laws in a ball, heat in a kettle, quantum physics in a phone and relativity in a satellite map.

beats.scene: A girl on a hill at dusk tosses a ball beneath the first stars
beats.summary: A few ideas, patiently tested, connect a thrown ball to the stars, and many questions remain open.

B1B2: Why does a ball fall down, and why does a hot drink get cold? Physics is the science that looks for simple answers to questions like these.
A leaf, a raindrop and a ball look like three different things. Yet physics says that a few simple rules explain how all of them move.
To study the world, you must first measure it. Length is measured in metres, and a metre is the same distance in every country.
Time is measured in seconds, and a whole day holds 86,400 of them. A stopwatch lets you measure a short event, such as a race, very exactly.
How much matter is there inside a heavy stone or a feather? That amount is called its mass, and we measure it in kilograms, using a scale like the one in a shop.
If you time the same fall three times, you will probably get three slightly different answers. Scientists repeat a measurement and take the average, and they are honest about how sure they are.
If a car travels sixty kilometres in one hour, its speed is sixty kilometres an hour. To find a speed, you simply divide the distance by the time.
A speedometer shows your speed at one moment, not over the whole trip. On a long ride you may go very slowly uphill and very fast downhill, and the average hides both.
Speed tells you how fast, but not which way. Velocity is speed together with a direction, so two walkers going opposite ways have different velocities even at the same speed.
Physicists often draw a graph of distance against time. A steep line shows something moving fast, and a flat line shows that it has stopped.
Acceleration means a change in speed, and it can mean slowing down as well as speeding up. That is why you feel pressed into your seat when a car pulls away quickly.
When a bus brakes, everyone standing on it leans forward. Slowing down is also an acceleration, but it points the opposite way from speeding up.
Velocity includes direction, so a car that turns a corner at a steady speed is still accelerating. That is why you feel pushed sideways in a bend.
As a lift begins to rise, you feel a little heavier for a moment. When it slows near the top, you feel a little lighter.
A stone that falls from a bridge does not fall at a steady speed. It gets faster every second, gaining about ten metres a second of speed each time.
For many centuries people believed that heavy objects fall faster than light ones, because that is how it often looks. About four hundred years ago, Galileo argued that this was a mistake.
Falling was too fast to measure in his day, so Galileo rolled balls down gentle slopes instead. He found that the balls gained speed steadily as they rolled.
In air, a feather drifts down much more slowly than a coin. The reason is not weight, but the air, which pushes back harder against wide, light things.
In 1971 an astronaut on the Moon dropped a hammer and a feather together. There is no air there, so both reached the ground at the same moment.
A skydiver speeds up at first, but the air pushes back harder as she goes faster. In the end she stops speeding up, and a parachute makes that final speed much smaller.
Isaac Newton was an English scientist who lived about three hundred and fifty years ago. In 1687 he published a famous book that explained motion with three simple rules.
A puck on very smooth ice slides a long way, and very little slows it down. Newton's first law says that a moving object keeps going in a straight line unless a force stops it.
Put a coin on a card above a glass, then flick the card sideways. The coin stays where it was for a moment and drops straight down into the glass, because things resist a change in their motion.
If a car stops suddenly, your body keeps moving forward at the old speed. A seat belt applies a gentle force that slows you down together with the car.
Push an empty trolley and it speeds up quickly. Give it the same push when it is full of shopping and it speeds up much more slowly.
If you double the push, the acceleration is doubled too. If you double the mass, it is halved, and the unit of force is named the newton, after Isaac Newton.
A swimmer pushes the water backwards, and the water pushes her forwards with an equal force. Newton's third law says that forces always come in pairs.

A rocket throws burning gas downwards at great speed, and the gas pushes the rocket upwards in return. This works even in empty space, because the rocket pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.
When you walk, your foot pushes backwards against the ground, and the ground pushes you forwards. On smooth ice that push is weak, and your foot slides away instead.
Push a wall while wearing roller skates, and you will roll away backwards. The wall pushes you, and your push acts on the wall, so the two forces do not cancel out.
Newton's first law seems wrong when you push a box across a floor, because the box soon stops. The reason is friction, a rubbing force between the box and the floor that slows it down.
Friction is not just a nuisance, because we could not live without it. It lets your shoes grip the ground, your hands hold a cup and a car stop at a red light.
Rub your hands together hard and they soon feel warm. Friction changes the energy of motion into heat, and that is also how people once started fires with sticks.
A famous story says that Newton watched an apple fall and began to wonder about the Moon. He realised that the pull that brings the apple down might also reach as far as the Moon.
Newton's law of gravity says that every object pulls on every other one. The pull is stronger when the objects are heavier, and it gets weaker as they move further apart.
You pull on the person next to you, but the force is far too weak to notice. Around 1798 an English scientist named Henry Cavendish measured such a tiny pull between lead balls.
Newton imagined a cannon on a very high mountain. Fire the ball faster and faster, and it lands further away, until at last it falls around the Earth and never lands.
The space station circles the Earth about every ninety minutes. The astronauts float because they and the station are falling together, not because there is no gravity there.
A bag of apples has the same mass on the Moon as on Earth, but it feels much lighter there. Mass is the amount of matter, while weight is the pull of gravity on it.
The Moon pulls on the Earth's oceans, and the water bulges towards it. As the Earth turns, most coasts see two high tides and two low tides each day.
Energy is the ability to make things change, and it comes in many forms. A boiling pot, a moving bicycle and a glowing lamp all use energy in their own way.
The energy of a moving thing is called kinetic energy. It grows with the mass, and even faster with the speed, so a car at double the speed has four times the energy.
When you lift a book onto a high shelf, you store energy in it. This stored energy is called potential energy, and it is released as movement if the book falls.
At the top of a swing, you stop for a moment and have the most stored energy. At the bottom you move fastest, and the stored energy has become energy of motion.
A roller coaster is pulled slowly to the top of its first hill, and then it races down using the stored energy. Energy is never created or destroyed, but it keeps changing from one form to another.
In physics, work means pushing or pulling something over a distance. When you carry a heavy bag up the stairs, you do work, and you transfer energy from your body to the bag.
Power tells you how quickly energy is used by a machine or a person. It is measured in watts, so a hundred watt bulb uses energy ten times as fast as a ten watt bulb.
Food contains chemical energy that your body slowly releases. Many adults need roughly two thousand kilocalories a day, although the exact amount depends on the person.
Wood, petrol and batteries all store energy in their chemicals. When the chemicals react, the energy comes out as heat, light or electricity.
A bouncing ball never bounces back to its full height. Each bounce turns a little of its energy into heat and sound, and the energy spreads out into the floor and the air.
A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a point. Push down on the long end, and the short end lifts a much heavier load, although you must move your end much further.
More than two thousand years ago, a Greek scientist named Archimedes worked out how levers behave. He is said to have boasted that, with a long enough lever, he could move the whole world.
On a seesaw, a heavy child sitting close to the middle can be balanced by a light child sitting far out at the end. It is the distance as well as the weight that counts.
A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it, and it lets you pull down to lift something up. With several pulleys together you need less force, but you must pull a longer length of rope.
Lifting a heavy barrel straight up is very hard, but pushing it up a ramp is much easier. The longer and gentler the ramp is, the smaller the push you need.
An axe is a wedge, which turns a push forwards into a strong push to the sides. A screw is really a ramp wrapped around a rod, so a gentle turn can drive it with great force.
Gears are wheels with teeth that fit together and turn each other. A small gear that drives a big one turns it more slowly but with greater force.
A fat handle on a thin shaft is called a wheel and axle. It works like a lever that goes round and round, and your hand has to move further than the tip does.
A bicycle is really a bundle of many simple machines put together. Its pedals are levers, its wheels turn on axles, and its gears let you choose between an easy push and a faster ride.
No machine can give you more energy than you put in. What you gain in force you always pay for in distance, and friction takes a little of the energy as heat.
Pressure is the force on each small piece of surface. A sharp knife has a tiny edge, so it cuts easily, while a wide snowshoe spreads your weight and stops you sinking into the snow.
Water has weight, so the deeper you go, the more water there is above you pushing down. That is why divers feel a pressure in their ears, and why dam walls are thicker at the bottom.
Pressure in a liquid is passed on to every part of it. In a garage lift, a small push on a narrow piston becomes a large force on a wide one, strong enough to lift a car.
A famous story says that Archimedes noticed the water spilling over as he got into his bath. He saw that an object pushes aside an amount of water equal to its own volume.
An object in water pushes some water aside, and the water pushes back up on it. If that push equals the object's weight, the object floats.
A block of steel sinks, but a ship made of the same steel floats. The ship's hull is mostly full of air, so the ship as a whole is lighter than the water it pushes aside.
A submarine has large tanks that it can fill with water or with air. With water in the tanks, the submarine becomes heavier and sinks, and with air in the tanks, it rises again.
Air feels like nothing, but it has weight, and it presses on everything. At sea level it presses with about one kilogram on every square centimetre, and on high mountains the pressure is much lower.
When you sip through a straw, you do not really pull the juice up. You lower the pressure inside the straw, and the air pressing on the juice outside pushes it upwards.
Hot air is lighter than the same amount of cool air. A hot-air balloon is pushed upwards by the cool air around it, just as water holds up a ship.
Everything is made of tiny particles that are always moving. Temperature tells you how fast they move on average, so hot tea has quicker particles than cold water.
A thermometer is a tool that measures how hot or cold something is. On the Celsius scale, which most of the world uses, water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees at sea level.

If temperature measures how fast particles move, then there must be a coldest temperature at which they hardly move at all. It is called absolute zero, and it is about minus two hundred and seventy-three degrees Celsius.
Ice, water and steam are made of exactly the same tiny particles. In ice they are held in place, in water they slide past each other, and in steam they fly about freely.
Melting ice takes in a lot of heat, yet its temperature does not rise until the last piece has melted. The energy goes into breaking the ice's pattern apart, not into speeding the particles up.
Even below boiling point, the fastest particles at the surface of water can escape into the air. This is evaporation, and because the fast ones leave, what is left becomes cooler.

When something is heated, its particles move more widely, and the whole object grows a little bigger. Engineers leave small gaps in bridges and railway tracks so that they can expand safely in summer.

In conduction, fast-moving particles pass their energy to their neighbours, and heat travels along. Metals do this very well, so a metal spoon in hot soup warms up quickly, while a wooden one does not.
Warm air is lighter than cool air, so it rises, while the cooler air sinks to take its place. This loop of moving air carries heat around a room, and it is called convection.

You can feel the warmth of a fire on your face even when the air between is cold. Heat can travel as waves of radiation, and it needs no material to carry it, which is how the Sun's warmth crosses space.
Insulation is the way we slow down the flow of heat. A woolly jumper traps still air, which conducts heat badly, and a flask has a near-empty space between its walls that blocks heat even more.
A cup of hot coffee always cools down until it is as warm as the room. It never takes heat from the cool air and gets hotter by itself.
Pour hot water into cold water and you quickly get warm water. You will never see the warm water separate by itself into a hot part and a cold part.
Think of a new pack of cards in perfect order and a pack that has been shuffled. There are far more ways to be mixed up than to be in order, and physicists call this measure entropy.

In a steam engine, a fire heats water into steam, and the expanding steam pushes a piston. This invention turned heat into motion, and it powered factories, ships and trains in the nineteenth century.
No engine can turn all of its heat into useful motion. Some must always be released to the cooler air, and a typical petrol car wastes most of the energy in its fuel as heat.
For centuries inventors tried to build machines that would run for ever without any fuel. Every attempt failed, because energy is never created and some of it always spreads out as heat.
A fridge does not make cold, it moves heat. It pumps heat out of the cold inside and releases it into your kitchen, which is why the back of a fridge feels warm.
A dropped egg breaks, but a broken egg never jumps back together. The laws of motion work either way, so entropy is what gives time its one-way direction.
Entropy rises in a closed system, but the Earth is not closed. Sunlight brings in energy that feeds plants and drives the weather, and the Earth sends heat back out into space.
When a pebble falls into a pond, ripples spread outwards. A floating leaf only bobs up and down, which shows that the wave carries energy but does not carry the water along.
A wave has high points called crests and low points called troughs. The distance between two crests is the wavelength, and the number of crests passing each second is the frequency, counted in hertz.

If you shake a rope up and down, the wave moves along it, and the rope moves sideways. In a stretched spring, you can also push and pull the coils, so that the wave squeezes and stretches along its path.
When a guitar string is plucked, it shakes quickly backwards and forwards. It pushes the air next to it, and the vibration travels through the air as a wave until it reaches your ear.
If you ring a bell inside a glass jar and pump the air out, the sound slowly fades away. Sound needs air or something else to travel through, so in the emptiness of space it cannot cross.
Sound moves through air at about three hundred and forty metres a second, which is slow compared with light. That is why you see lightning first, and hear the thunder a few seconds later.
A short, thin string vibrates fast and gives a high note, while a long, thick one vibrates slowly and gives a low note. How loud a sound is depends on the energy of the wave, not on its pitch.
A shout in a valley bounces off the far cliff and comes back to you as an echo. Bats use echoes to find insects in the dark, and ships use them to measure how deep the sea is.

A passing ambulance siren seems to drop in pitch as it goes by. Moving towards you, it squeezes the sound waves together, and moving away, it stretches them out, and this is called the Doppler effect.
Every object has a natural rhythm at which it likes to swing. If you push a swing in time with that rhythm, even small pushes build up into a big motion, and this is called resonance.
Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres a second, faster than anything else we know. It takes a little over eight minutes to reach us from the Sun.
Light travels in straight lines, so when something blocks it, a shadow forms behind. The shadow of a stick on a sundial moves as the Sun crosses the sky, and it tells the time.
Space is so large that astronomers measure it in light-years, the distance light covers in one year. That is about nine and a half million million kilometres.
A mirror bounces light back in a very regular way, so that the angle at which light arrives equals the angle at which it leaves. A rough surface scatters the light, and so it gives no clear picture.
Around 1666, Newton sent sunlight through a glass prism and saw a band of colours appear. He showed that white light is really a mixture of colours, and that glass sorts them out.
A rainbow is made when sunlight goes into raindrops, bounces off the back, and comes out again. Each colour is bent a little differently, so the colours spread out into a bow.
An apple looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs most of the other colours. A black cat absorbs almost all the light, while a white sheet reflects almost all of it.
Light bends when it passes from one material into another, such as from water into air. This is called refraction, and it is why a spoon in a glass of water looks bent.
A lens is a curved piece of glass that bends light to a point. Spectacles help people see clearly, and your eye has a lens of its own that focuses light.
A telescope uses lenses to make faraway things look near, and a microscope makes tiny things look big. In 1610, Galileo used a telescope to see four moons moving around the planet Jupiter.
When you rub a balloon on your hair, tiny electric charges move from one to the other. The charged balloon can then attract your hair or stick to a wall.
There are two kinds of electric charge, which we call positive and negative. Charges that are different attract each other, and charges that are the same push each other apart.
Lightning is a giant electric spark that jumps from a cloud to the ground. The air along its path becomes several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

Electricity moves easily through metals, which are called conductors, because they contain electrons that can move freely. Plastic and rubber are insulators, so they are used to cover wires and keep us safe.
In 1800, an Italian scientist named Alessandro Volta built the first battery from a pile of metal discs. For the first time, people could make a steady flow of electricity whenever they wished.
An electric current is a flow of charge, and it needs a complete loop to move around. If you break the loop anywhere, the bulb goes out.
Imagine electricity as water flowing along a pipe between two tanks. Voltage is the push, and current is how much flows each second, counted in amperes.
Some materials resist the flow of current more than others. A thin wire in a bulb resists strongly, so it grows hot and glows, and the same thing heats the wires in a toaster.

In a series circuit the current has only one path, so one broken bulb stops all of them. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own path, and the others stay lit, which is how the sockets of a house are connected.

A fuse is a thin wire that melts if too much current passes through it. A circuit breaker does the same job by switching off, and mains electricity can be dangerous, so it must be treated with great care.
A magnet pulls on objects that are made of iron, such as a nail. Every magnet has two ends, called poles, and two north poles push each other away, while a north and a south pole pull together.
A magnet has an invisible magnetic field all around it. If you sprinkle iron filings on paper above a magnet, they line up along curved lines that show the shape of the field.
A compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with the magnetic field of the Earth. This shows that our planet itself behaves like a giant magnet, with a pole near each end.
The Sun sends out charged particles, and the Earth's magnetic field steers them towards the poles. There they hit the air high above us, and the air glows in coloured lights called the aurora.
In 1820, a Danish scientist named Hans Christian Oersted noticed something surprising. A compass needle moved when it was near a wire that carried a current.
If you wind a wire into a coil around a piece of iron and send current through it, you get an electromagnet. It can be switched on to pick up scrap metal and then switched off to drop it.
A magnet pushes on a wire that carries a current. In an electric motor, this force is used to turn a coil round and round, so that electrical energy becomes motion.
In 1831, Michael Faraday tried the opposite experiment to the one by Oersted. He moved a magnet in and out of a coil of wire, and a current flowed in the wire, even though there was no battery.
A generator spins a magnet inside coils of wire to make a current. Wind, falling water or steam can turn the generator, and this is how most of our electricity is made.
Electricity is carried over long distances at a very high voltage, because that wastes less energy as heat in the wires. Near our homes, transformers lower the voltage to a safe level.
In the 1860s, a Scottish scientist named James Clerk Maxwell wrote down one set of rules for electricity and magnetism. His rules predicted waves that travel at the speed of light.

In 1887, the German physicist Heinrich Hertz made invisible waves with an electric spark and detected them across his laboratory. They behaved just as Maxwell had predicted, and so Maxwell's idea was proved right.
Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields, and it is only one member of a large family. Radio waves, microwaves and X-rays are the same kind of wave with different lengths.
Radio waves are the longest waves in the family, and they pass easily through walls. A radio, a television and a mobile phone all use them to carry sound, pictures and messages through the air.
A microwave oven uses waves a little shorter than radio waves. They make the water in your food shake, and the shaking warms the food from the inside out.

Every warm object gives out infrared radiation, which we cannot see but can feel as heat. In 1800 the astronomer William Herschel discovered it, and special cameras can now see in the dark by using it.
Visible light covers a tiny slice of the family of waves, with wavelengths between about four hundred and seven hundred billionths of a metre. Red has the longest waves and violet has the shortest.
Beyond violet lies ultraviolet light, which our eyes cannot see. It can burn your skin and harm your eyes, and the ozone layer high above us blocks most of it, while sun cream blocks more.
X-rays are very short waves that pass through soft parts of the body but are stopped by bones. The German scientist Wilhelm Röntgen discovered them in 1895, and they let doctors see inside people.
Gamma rays are the shortest waves of all, and they carry the most energy. They come from radioactive atoms and from violent events in space, and they can also be used in hospitals to treat illness.
Everything around you is made of atoms, and each one is far too small to see. Hundreds of thousands of atoms could sit side by side across the width of a single hair.
More than two thousand years ago, the Greek thinker Democritus suggested that everything is made of tiny pieces that cannot be cut. He called them atoms, but he had no way to prove it.

In 1827 a scientist named Robert Brown saw tiny grains of pollen moving about in water. In 1905 Einstein explained that water molecules were bumping them, and this convinced many people that atoms are real.
There are only about ninety different kinds of atom in nature, and each kind is called an element. Hydrogen is the lightest, and uranium is the heaviest of those found in nature.
In 1897 the English physicist Joseph John Thomson discovered the electron. It was far lighter than the lightest atom, so it proved that atoms are not the smallest things after all.
Around 1909, Ernest Rutherford's team fired tiny particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back, which showed that each atom has a very small, heavy centre.
An atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny nucleus at its centre. If the nucleus were a pea in the middle of a large stadium, the electrons would be specks whirling around the outer seats.
Atoms join together by sharing or swapping their outer electrons, and a group of joined atoms is called a molecule. A molecule of water has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Some atoms have nuclei that are unstable, and they break apart by themselves, giving out energy. This is called radioactivity, and a half-life is the time it takes for half of a sample to change.
The Sun shines because its core is hot enough to join hydrogen nuclei into helium, which is called fusion. Power stations on Earth work the other way and split heavy nuclei, which is called fission.
Maxwell's theory gave one fixed speed for light, and that puzzled physicists. In the 1880s, careful experiments looked for a difference caused by the Earth's motion, and they found none.
In 1905 a young man called Albert Einstein was working in a patent office in Switzerland. In his spare time he wrote several papers that changed physics for ever.
Einstein simply accepted the strange puzzle, and asked what follows from it. Everyone gets the same answer when they measure light's speed, even a runner chasing a beam.
If the speed of light is the same for everyone, then time itself must behave strangely. A clock on a train moving at very high speed ticks more slowly than a clock on the platform.

Imagine a clock that ticks each time a light beam bounces between two mirrors. If the clock is moving, the light has to travel a longer slanting path, but its speed is the same, so each tick takes longer.
In 1971, scientists flew very exact atomic clocks around the world in aeroplanes. When they compared them with clocks on the ground, the tiny differences matched what relativity predicts.
The speed of light is a limit for anything that has mass. The faster an object goes, the harder it is to speed it up, so reaching the limit would need endless energy.

Relativity has another very strange consequence for our ordinary ideas about time. Two events that seem simultaneous to one person can happen at different times for another, so there is no shared now.
Einstein also found that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. His famous equation says that the energy in a piece of matter equals its mass times the speed of light multiplied by itself.
The Sun turns about four million tonnes of its mass into light and heat every second. It is so huge that it has lost only a tiny fraction of its mass in billions of years.
Special relativity did not fit with Newton's law of gravity, and that troubled Einstein. He worked for about ten years on a new theory of gravity, and he finished it in 1915.
Einstein imagined a person falling freely inside a closed lift. Nothing would press him to the floor, and he and everything around him would float, so gravity and acceleration seemed closely linked.
In general relativity, gravity is not a pulling force. A heavy object like the Sun bends space and time around it, and planets follow the curved paths that result.
Relativity joins space and time into one thing called spacetime. A saying sums it up: matter tells spacetime how to bend, and bent spacetime tells matter how to move.

In 1919, the astronomer Arthur Eddington photographed stars beside the Sun during a total eclipse. Their light was bent by just the amount that Einstein had predicted, and Einstein became world famous.
Relativity says that time runs more slowly where gravity is stronger. A clock on the ground ticks a tiny bit slower than one at the top of a tall tower, and exact clocks show this.

The satellites of the global positioning system, known as GPS, carry very exact clocks. Engineers must correct them for both kinds of relativity, or your phone's map would be wrong by kilometres within a day.
A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that not even light can get out. It can form when a very massive star runs out of fuel and collapses under its own weight.
In 2019, astronomers released the first picture of a black hole. It showed a dark centre ringed by glowing gas, and a picture of the black hole in our own galaxy followed in 2022.
In September 2015, two detectors in the United States felt a tiny shiver in space itself. It came from two black holes that had merged more than a billion years earlier.
A hot piece of metal glows, and its colour changes as it gets hotter. Old physics could not explain this, until Max Planck suggested in 1900 that energy comes in small separate packets.
In 1905, Einstein explained why light can knock electrons out of metal. He said that light comes in separate packets, now called photons, and each packet can free just one electron.

Electrons in an atom can have only certain energies, as if standing on the steps of a ladder. When they drop down a step, they give out light of one exact colour, so each element has its own pattern of colours.
A ball on a smooth slope can stop at any height, but a ball on a staircase can stop only on the steps. Quantum theory says that many things in nature behave like the staircase.

If you shine light through two narrow slits, you do not get two bright lines on the screen. You get a pattern of many bright and dark stripes, because waves from the two slits add together and cancel each other.

When single electrons are sent through two slits one at a time, each lands on the screen as a single dot. After thousands of dots, the stripes appear, as if each electron had gone through both slits like a wave.
In 1927, Werner Heisenberg showed that you cannot know both the position and the motion of a tiny particle exactly. This is not a fault in our instruments, but a basic fact about nature.
Quantum theory cannot say exactly when one radioactive atom will break up. It can only say how likely this is, and scientists still argue about what these chances really mean.
In 1935, Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat in a sealed box, linked to a single atom that might or might not decay. He wanted to show how odd it sounds to apply quantum rules to everyday things.

Quantum physics may seem far from daily life, but it explains how lasers, transistors and computer chips work. It is also used in medical scanners and in atomic clocks, and scientists are working on quantum computers.

Near Geneva, a ring-shaped tunnel about twenty-seven kilometres around holds the Large Hadron Collider. It smashes protons together at almost the speed of light, so that scientists can look at what they are made of.

Physicists have a list of the basic particles that make up everything we know. It is called the Standard Model, and it includes six kinds of quark, the electron and its relatives, and particles that carry forces.
Physics finds that there are just four basic forces. They are gravity, electromagnetism, the strong force that holds the nucleus together, and the weak force that causes some kinds of radioactivity.
In 2012, scientists at CERN announced that they had found the Higgs particle. It had been predicted in 1964, and it is a sign of a field that gives mass to other particles.
Every kind of particle has an opposite twin called an antiparticle. When a particle meets its twin, both vanish in a flash of energy, and hospitals use this effect in scanners.
