The Sun is one star among hundreds of billions in our galaxy, the Milky Way. Telescopes show us that our galaxy is just one of hundreds of billions of galaxies in the universe.

In the 1920s, astronomers including Edwin Hubble measured the light from distant galaxies. They found that almost all of them are moving away, and that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it goes.
If the galaxies are moving apart, then long ago they were close together. Scientists believe it began hot and dense close to fourteen billion years ago, and its faint afterglow can still be detected.

The stars at the edge of a galaxy move so fast that the visible matter could not hold them in. Scientists think there is unseen dark matter that gives extra pull, but nobody has yet detected it directly.
Ordinary matter is only about five percent of the universe. About a quarter is dark matter, and most of the rest is dark energy, which speeds up the expansion of the universe.
Physics works because every idea has to be tested by experiments. A good theory must predict something that an experiment could show to be wrong, and the best theories survive many such tests.

Uranus did not follow the path that Newton's laws predicted. In 1846, a French mathematician named Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unseen planet must be, and astronomers found Neptune right there.

The orbit of Mercury drifts by a tiny amount that Newton's laws could not explain. Some astronomers suggested another hidden planet, but none was ever found, and in 1915 Einstein's new theory explained the drift exactly.

In 2011 an experiment in Italy seemed to show tiny particles travelling faster than light. After weeks of checking, the team found a loose cable, and when it was fixed, the strange result disappeared.
A new result is not trusted until other teams, working separately, can repeat it. Physicists also demand very strong evidence, so that the chance of a lucky accident is tiny.
General relativity describes the huge, and quantum theory describes the tiny, and both work extremely well. But nobody has yet found a single theory of gravity that combines them.
Several ideas, such as string theory and loop quantum gravity, try to join gravity and quantum theory. They are mathematically beautiful, but none of them has yet been confirmed by an experiment.
Many questions are still open, such as what dark matter and dark energy really are. Nobody knows why there is more matter than antimatter, or what happened at the very start of the universe.
Everything in this book is at work in an ordinary day. Heat boils the kettle, electricity runs the fridge, quantum physics powers the phone chip, and relativity helps your map find you.
You began with a ball and a hot cup of tea, and you have ended among galaxies and atoms. The same few ideas, patiently tested, connect them all, and there is much left to discover.
C1C2: Physics begins with ordinary wonder: why a thrown ball comes down, why a kettle boils, why the sky glows at the end of the day. Its great surprise is that a handful of ideas, pursued patiently, can explain an astonishing share of what happens. This book takes those ideas one at a time, starting with the simplest and ending at the edge of what nobody yet understands.

At first glance a drifting leaf, a streaking raindrop and a thrown ball have nothing in common. Physics is the habit of looking past those differences until a single rule appears underneath them all. Once you have found one such rule, you will start to notice it everywhere, working quietly behind the ordinary scenes of the day.

Nothing in physics can begin until something has been measured, because a number can be checked by anyone while an impression can only be argued over. Length is measured in metres, and a kilometre is a thousand of them, so that a distance written down in one country means exactly the same thing in another. That shared agreement is quietly one of the greatest achievements in the whole history of science.

Time is counted in seconds, and a single day contains exactly 86,400 of them, which is why a second feels so small and so quick. Early clocks could only count minutes at best, but modern watches measure fractions of a second without any effort. Whenever a physicist wants to know how fast something happens, a trustworthy measurement of time is where the answer begins.

Mass is the amount of matter packed into an object, and it is counted in kilograms. A shop's scale compares the apples in its pan with a set of agreed standards, so the buyer and the seller trust the same number. Strictly speaking a scale measures weight, but for now the difference does not matter, and we will return to it later in the book.

No measurement is ever perfectly exact, because a hand is a little late on the button and a tape sags a little in the middle. Careful scientists therefore repeat each measurement many times, take an average and state how far it might be wrong. That honesty about uncertainty may seem like a weakness, yet it is exactly what makes a result trustworthy.

Speed is the simplest idea in the study of motion: it is the distance something covers divided by the time it takes. A cyclist who rides thirty kilometres in two hours has averaged fifteen kilometres an hour, even if she crawled up the hills and flew down the other side. Averages hide the details of the journey, which is why physicists also care deeply about how speed changes from moment to moment.

The number on a speedometer is a different thing from an average, because it reports how fast you are going at this very instant. A rider who labours up a hill at six kilometres an hour and then plunges down the other side at forty may still finish with a modest average. Both numbers are true, and each answers a different question about the same journey.

Speed on its own says nothing about where something is heading, and for many purposes the heading matters as much as the pace. Physicists therefore use velocity, which combines a speed with a direction, so that two walkers moving at the same pace in opposite directions have opposite velocities. This small refinement becomes essential as soon as we ask what makes things speed up, slow down or turn.

Long before computers, scientists learned to turn motion into a picture by drawing distance against time on a graph. A steep line then means a fast journey, a flat one means a pause and a curve means that the speed is changing as the line goes on. A good graph lets the eye see in a single glance what a page of numbers would hide.

Acceleration is the rate at which speed changes, and because direction matters too, turning a corner at a steady speed is acceleration as well. You feel it in your body: pressed into the seat as a car pulls away, thrown sideways when it takes a bend, lurching forward when it brakes. In every case it is the change, and not the motion itself, that you can feel.

A bus that brakes suddenly sends its standing passengers staggering towards the front, and the reason is not mysterious. Slowing down is simply acceleration in the direction opposite to the motion, and your body, still travelling at the old speed, wants to carry on as before. Physics treats a driver pressing the brake and a driver pressing the pedal as two sides of the same idea.

Because velocity includes direction, a vehicle that swings around a bend at a perfectly steady speed is still accelerating, since its velocity is changing all the way round. Passengers feel this as a sideways shove towards the outside of the curve, a sensation familiar to anyone who has sat in the back of a taxi. Speeding up, slowing down and turning are therefore three faces of a single idea.

Stand on a scale inside a lift and you will find that the number briefly changes as the lift begins to rise or to stop. The floor must push harder on you while you accelerate upwards, and softer while you slow down, which is exactly why your stomach seems to disagree with the motion. It is a neat demonstration that what we feel as heaviness is really the push of the floor beneath us.

A stone released from a bridge does not drop at a constant speed but accelerates, gaining about ten metres a second of speed with every second that passes. After one second it is moving at roughly ten metres a second, after two at about twenty, and after three at about thirty. The pull of the Earth never takes a rest, and so the stone keeps getting faster for as long as it falls through clear air.

For many centuries scholars taught that a heavy object must fall faster than a light one, and everyday experience seemed to agree. About four hundred years ago the Italian scientist Galileo challenged that belief with a clever piece of reasoning, imagining a heavy stone tied to a light one. If the light stone really slowed the heavy one down, he argued, then the pair, though heavier than either stone, would fall more slowly than the heavy one alone, and that made no sense.

A falling stone moves far too quickly to be timed with the clocks of Galileo's day, so he slowed the motion by letting balls roll down gentle wooden ramps. By measuring how far each ball travelled in equal moments, he discovered that its speed grew steadily instead of jumping about. The experiment shows a favourite trick of physics, which is to find a cleverly slow version of something that is too fast to study directly.

Drop a coin and a feather in a room and the coin wins by a long way, which seems to prove the old belief. The real cause is the air, which pushes back against a wide, light feather far more than against a small, dense coin, and a crumpled sheet of paper falls faster than a flat one for just the same reason. Take the air away completely, and the whole difference between the two objects simply disappears.

In 1971 an Apollo astronaut stood on the dusty grey Moon, held out a hammer and a feather at the same height and let go of both. With no air to hold the feather back, the two objects fell side by side and struck the ground at the very same instant, just as Galileo had reasoned centuries before. It was a rare case of a grand idea being tested in the most dramatic and remote laboratory imaginable.

A skydiver begins by speeding up like any falling object, but the faster she falls, the harder the air pushes back against her. Eventually the push of the air balances the pull of the Earth, and she settles at a steady top speed of roughly two hundred kilometres an hour. A parachute catches far more air, so the balance arrives at a much gentler speed, and she can step onto the ground safely.

Isaac Newton, born in England in 1642, was a solitary and fiercely curious young man who filled notebook after notebook with questions about the world. In 1687 he published a famous book that explained motion with just three rules, and its influence on science would last for centuries. Those three rules are simple enough to state in a sentence each, yet they describe the movement of nearly everything you can see.

A puck sent skimming across a smooth frozen lake glides for an astonishingly long distance, because almost nothing is there to slow it. Newton's first law captures what this suggests: an object that is moving carries on in a straight line at the same speed, and an object that is still stays still, unless a force acts on it. Motion needs no push to keep it alive, and only a change needs a cause.

Balance a coin on a card above a glass and flick the card away sharply, and the coin, apparently unmoved, drops neatly into the glass. This stubborn reluctance of things to change what they are doing is called inertia, and the heavier an object is, the more of it there is. The trick works because the card leaves so quickly that there is no time for friction to drag the coin along with it.

When a car meets a wall and stops almost at once, the people inside obey the first law and keep moving forward at the car's old speed. A seat belt is the force that Newton's rule demands, spreading the slowing across the strong parts of the body and over a longer moment of time. It is a plain example of how a rule discovered in the seventeenth century saves lives on every road today.

Push an empty shopping trolley and it leaps forward, but give a full one exactly the same push and it responds sluggishly. Newton's second law puts that everyday experience into plain words: a bigger force produces a bigger acceleration, while a bigger mass produces a smaller one. Every engineer who designs a car, a bridge or a rocket relies on this one relationship between push, mass and change of motion.

The second law is wonderfully tidy, because doubling the push doubles the acceleration, while doubling the mass cuts the acceleration in half. Force is measured in newtons, and a single newton is about the weight of a small apple, enough to make a one kilogram mass speed up by one metre a second every second. Having a clear unit meant that forces, once only a vague feeling of pushing and pulling, could finally be measured and compared.

A swimmer drives the water backwards with her hands and feet, and the water, in return, drives her forwards. Newton's third law says that forces always come in such pairs: whenever one body pushes on another, the second pushes back on the first with exactly the same strength in the opposite direction. You cannot give a push without receiving one, which is a fact worth remembering the next time you lean on a door.

A rocket hurls a stream of hot gas downwards at tremendous speed, and the third law ensures that the gas pushes the rocket upwards with an equal force. People once doubted that a rocket could work in the emptiness of space, imagining that it needed air to push against, but it needs only its own exhaust. In a sense, the fuel is both the source of the push and the very thing that is being pushed away.

Every step you take is a quiet application of the third law: your foot pushes backwards on the ground, and the ground, in return, pushes you forwards. On smooth ice the grip between shoe and surface is poor, so the backward push cannot take hold and the foot simply slips out from underneath you. Walking, it turns out, is something we can only do because the whole planet pushes back.

A boy on roller skates who pushes against a wall finds himself rolling smoothly away, though he thought he was the only one pushing. The wall pushes him back with a force equal to his own, and since the two forces of a pair act on different objects, they never cancel each other out. Understanding that point is the key to the third law, and it clears away much of the confusion that surrounds it.

If Newton were right, a pushed box ought to slide on for ever, yet in practice it halts after a short distance. The missing ingredient is friction, the rubbing force that appears wherever two surfaces touch and that always acts against the sliding. Once you notice it, you see how cleverly it had been hiding the first law from everyone for thousands of years.

It is easy to think of friction as an enemy, but a world without it would be almost impossible to live in. Shoes would slide from under us, knots would come undone, nails would fall out of walls and a car would never stop at a red light. Much of what we call grip, hold and stability is friction doing its quiet work.

Rub your hands together briskly and within seconds they glow with warmth, because friction converts the energy of motion into heat. People have used this fact for thousands of years to start fires by spinning one stick against another. The same effect heats a brake pad on a long hill and makes a shooting star blaze as a grain of rock rushes through the air.

A famous story tells us that Newton, resting in a garden, watched an apple fall and wondered how far the pull that brought it down might reach. His great insight was that the same force might hold the Moon in its path around the Earth, and the old divide between earthly and heavenly motion began to melt. Whether or not the apple really fell, the idea behind the story changed science for good.

Newton proposed that gravity is not confined to the Earth but is a pull acting between every pair of objects in the universe. The pull grows stronger with the masses involved and weaker with the distance between them, and it can be calculated with a single neat rule. For the first time the falling of an apple and the circling of a planet were governed by the same law.

Two people sitting side by side do pull gently on each other, but the force is so small that no sense could detect it. Only a planet has enough mass to make gravity obvious, and the weakness of the effect explains why it was long unnoticed between ordinary things. Around 1798 the careful English scientist Henry Cavendish measured the feeble pull between lead balls, a triumph of patience over difficulty.

Newton imagined a cannon on top of a mountain so tall that it rose above the air. A slow shot lands nearby, a faster one lands farther away, and a shot fired fast enough falls all the way around the curved Earth without ever reaching the ground. An orbit, in other words, is not an escape from gravity but a fall that keeps missing.

The International Space Station circles the Earth roughly every ninety minutes, at a height of about four hundred kilometres, where gravity is still strong. Its astronauts float because they and the station are falling around the planet together, so nothing presses them against the floor. Weightlessness is therefore not the absence of gravity at all, but the strange sensation of falling freely together with everything around you.

Carry a bag of apples to the Moon and it contains exactly as much matter as before, so its mass has not changed. Yet it feels about six times lighter, because the Moon's gravity is only about one sixth as strong as the Earth's, and weight is simply the pull of gravity on a mass. The distinction matters, since mass belongs to the object while weight depends on where the object happens to be.

The same law that holds the Moon in orbit also tugs on the Earth's oceans, drawing the water into a gentle bulge that follows the Moon around the planet. As the Earth turns beneath these bulges, most coastlines experience roughly two high tides and two low tides every day. Even the rhythm of the sea is a message from the sky, written by gravity.

Energy is a slippery idea, yet nothing in nature happens without it, because it is what makes things move, heat up, glow or change. It appears in many forms, such as the heat of a pot, the movement of a bicycle and the light of a lamp. The remarkable discovery of physics is that all these forms are really one thing wearing different clothes.

The energy that a moving object carries is known as kinetic energy, and it rises with both the mass and the speed. Because the speed is squared in the rule, a car travelling twice as fast carries four times as much energy, which is why high speeds are so dangerous. A modest increase in speed can therefore turn a minor bump into a serious crash.

Lift a heavy book onto a high shelf and you have done something more than move it, because you have stored energy in it. This stored energy, called potential energy, is waiting patiently, and if the book tumbles off the shelf, it turns into the energy of motion on the way down. Height, like a drawn bow or a squeezed spring, is a way of keeping energy in reserve.

At the highest point of its arc a swing pauses for an instant, and all of its energy is stored in its height. As it falls, that energy is steadily turned into motion, so that at the bottom the swing moves fastest, and then the motion is turned back into height on the far side. The whole ride is a graceful exchange between two kinds of energy, and no new push is needed to keep the swap going.

A roller coaster spends the first minute of its journey being hauled slowly to the top of a hill, and the rest of the ride spending the energy stored there. Physicists call this the conservation of energy: it is never created and never destroyed, but only changed from one form into another. Every careful measurement ever made has agreed with that statement, which makes it one of the most trusted rules in all of science.

To a physicist, work has a precise meaning: it is what a force does when it moves something through a distance. A person climbing a staircase with a heavy bag does work against gravity, passing energy from the body to the bag in the form of height. The harder the push and the longer the distance, the more work is done, and the more energy has been moved.

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, and it is measured in watts, named after the Scottish engineer James Watt. Two machines may do exactly the same job, but the more powerful one gets it done sooner, and a hundred watt bulb gobbles energy ten times faster than a ten watt one. Whenever you see a number in watts on an appliance, it is telling you how hungry that machine is.

Every meal is a delivery of chemical energy, which the body releases in small steps to keep us warm, moving and thinking. Many adults use roughly two thousand kilocalories a day, although the exact figure varies a great deal with size, age and activity. A human being is, among other things, a very gentle engine that runs on bread, rice and fruit.

A log, a tank of petrol and a battery have little in common at first sight, yet each stores energy in the arrangement of its chemicals. When those chemicals react, the energy emerges as heat and light in the fire, as motion in the engine and as electricity in the battery. Chemical energy is potential energy of a different kind, locked in the very structure of matter.

A ball never rises as high as it started, because every bounce transforms a little of its energy into sound and into heat that warms the ball and the floor. The energy has not vanished, but it has spread into countless tiny motions that can no longer be gathered up again. This slow leakage into warmth is the fate of nearly all energy, and it will matter a great deal when we come to heat.

A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point, and with a long enough one a small push can raise a very heavy stone. What you gain in force you pay for in distance, since your end of the bar must travel much farther than the load does. The lever does not make energy appear from nowhere, but only trades one kind of effort for another.

More than two thousand years ago the Greek scientist Archimedes of Syracuse worked out exactly how a lever behaves. He is said to have boasted that, given a lever long enough and a place to stand, he could move the entire world, though the story was written down long after his death. The boast was safe from any test, but the idea behind it was perfectly sound.

A seesaw is a lever that children can sit on, and it demonstrates that weight is only half of the story. A heavy child sitting close to the middle can be balanced perfectly by a lighter one perched at the far end, because what matters is the weight multiplied by its distance from the pivot. Archimedes understood that rule perfectly well, and it still governs the way that cranes, scales and crowbars work today.

A single pulley, a grooved wheel with a rope running over it, changes only the direction of a pull, letting you haul downwards in order to lift upwards. Combine several wheels and the load is shared among the strands of rope, so that a small force can lift a large weight, though the rope you pull must be correspondingly longer. Once again, the machine trades force for distance, and nothing is gained for free.

Lifting a heavy barrel straight onto a lorry would defeat most people, yet rolling it up a long ramp is a manageable task. The ramp spreads the same rise over a greater distance, so the push needed at any moment is much smaller, and the longer and gentler the slope, the lighter the effort. Mountain roads wind back and forth in long zigzags across the hillside for just this reason.

An axe blade is a wedge, a ramp in disguise that converts a downward blow into powerful sideways forces that split the wood apart. A screw is another disguised ramp, in this case wrapped around a rod, so that many gentle turns of the head produce a strong grip over a very short distance. Once you know to look for ramps, you find them hiding in knives, zips, drills and the lids of jars.

Gears are wheels with interlocking teeth, and they pass motion from one part of a machine to another with hardly any slipping. When a small gear drives a larger one, the larger turns more slowly but with more turning force, and when the roles are reversed the speed rises at the cost of strength. Every clock, every drill and every car gearbox depends on this tidy trade between speed and strength.

A screwdriver with a thick handle turns a screw more easily than a thin one, and the reason is a lever that goes round and round. The wide handle is a wheel and the narrow blade an axle, so a small force applied over a large circle becomes a strong twist applied over a small one. Door knobs, taps and the steering wheels of cars work in the same way.

A bicycle is a collection of simple machines working in harmony: levers in the pedals, wheels turning on axles, and a chain connecting gears of different sizes. On a steep hill the rider chooses a low gear, which demands less force on the pedals but many more turns of them, while on a flat road a high gear covers more ground with every turn. The machine does not lighten the journey so much as let the rider choose how to pay for it.

All of the simple machines, from the lever to the bicycle, share one iron rule: none of them can deliver more energy than you put into it. What you gain in force you lose in distance, and the real machines in our world lose a little more to friction, which warms the moving parts. The dream of getting something for nothing has fascinated inventors for centuries, and it has never once come true.

Pressure is the force pressing on every small patch of a surface, found by dividing the force by the area it covers. A knife cuts because all of your push is squeezed onto an edge almost too thin to see, whereas a snowshoe spreads your weight over a wide frame and keeps you on top of the drift. The same push can therefore do something dramatic or almost nothing, depending only on where it lands.

The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you, and the pressure grows steadily with every metre that you descend. Divers feel it at once as a squeezing in the ears, and engineers answer it by building dam walls far thicker at the base than at the crest. In the deepest oceans the pressure is about a thousand times greater than at the surface, enough to crush a hollow metal object that is not strongly built.

A liquid cannot be squeezed into a smaller space, so pressure applied at one point is passed on undiminished to every other part of it. A hydraulic lift uses this fact by joining a narrow piston to a wide one, so that a gentle push on the first becomes a powerful lift on the second. It is the lever's old bargain in a new form, since the small piston must travel a long way to raise the big one a short way.

According to a famous story, the Greek scholar Archimedes was lowering himself into a bath when he noticed the water spilling over the edge and suddenly grasped a powerful idea. An object pushes aside exactly its own volume of water, which gave him a way to measure the size of an awkward shape without any calculation. Historians doubt that the tale is true in every detail, but the principle behind it is perfectly real.

When anything is lowered into water, it pushes some of the water out of the way, and the water pushes back upwards with a force equal to the weight of what was displaced. If that upward push can match the object's own weight, the object floats, and if it cannot, the object sinks. This tidy rule, often credited to Archimedes, explains every raft, ship and swimmer in the world.

A solid lump of steel sinks like a stone, yet a ship made of tens of thousands of tonnes of the same metal rides high on the waves. The secret is shape: the hull encloses an enormous volume of air, so the whole ship pushes aside a great deal of water for a modest weight. A ship floats not because steel is light, but because the ship is mostly empty space.

A submarine controls its depth by changing its own weight, which it does by flooding or emptying large tanks inside its hull. Let the sea in, and the vessel becomes slightly heavier than the water it displaces and sinks, but blow the water out with compressed air, and it becomes lighter and rises towards the light. Knowing exactly how much to add or remove is the art of every submarine crew.

Air seems to weigh nothing at all, yet the tall column of it above our heads presses on every square centimetre of us with a force of about one kilogram. We never feel the load, because the pressure inside our bodies pushes outwards just as hard. On the summit of Mount Everest there is much less air above, so the pressure there is only about a third of the pressure at sea level.

It feels as if you are pulling juice up a straw, but what really happens is that you remove some of the air from the inside, lowering the pressure there. The air pressing down on the juice in the glass is then stronger than the air in the straw, and it shoves the juice up into your mouth. In this sense, drinking is a gentle application of the weight of the atmosphere.

Heated air expands, so a balloon full of it weighs less than the cooler air it pushes out of the way, and the surrounding atmosphere lifts it much as water lifts a ship. The pilot climbs by firing the burner and descends by letting the air cool, never doing anything but adjusting that balance. We live at the bottom of an ocean of air, and a balloon is simply a boat that sails in it.

Everything around us is made of particles too small to see, and they are never still, jostling and vibrating all the time. Temperature is a measure of how energetically they move on average, so the particles in a mug of hot tea race about faster than those in a mug of cold water. Heat, then, is not a mysterious fluid but simply motion on a scale we cannot see.

A thermometer turns the invisible motion of particles into a number you can read, and the Celsius scale chooses two memorable markers for it. Pure water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees at ordinary sea-level pressure, and everything else is measured in between or beyond. Because the markers are tied to a substance everyone can obtain, a reading in Paris means the same as one in Tokyo.

If temperature is really the motion of particles, then there must be a limit to how cold anything can get, because particles cannot move more slowly than hardly at all. That limit is absolute zero, about two hundred and seventy-three degrees below zero on the Celsius scale, and laboratories have come astonishingly close to it without ever quite reaching it. Cold, it turns out, has a floor, while heat has no ceiling that we know of.

Ice, liquid water and steam are one and the same substance in three different states, distinguished only by how much energy the particles have. In ice they are locked into a rigid pattern and merely tremble, in water they slip freely past one another, and in steam they dash about with almost no attachment to their neighbours. Add enough energy and a solid turns into a liquid, and then into a gas.

A glass of ice and water stays at zero degrees however much heat flows in, until the very last cube has melted. The energy is not making the particles move faster but is being used to pull them out of their rigid arrangement, and the same thing happens when a kettle boils. This hidden energy, spent on changing the state of matter and not on raising the temperature, is why ice is such an effective way to cool a drink.

Water does not need to boil to turn into vapour, for the fastest particles at its surface can break free at almost any temperature. Each escaping particle carries away more than its share of energy, so the liquid left behind grows cooler, and that is exactly how sweat cools the body on a hot day. A puddle vanishing in the sun and a runner being chilled by a breeze are the same phenomenon.

As the particles in a solid vibrate more vigorously they push slightly farther apart, so nearly every material expands when it is heated and shrinks again as it cools. The effect is small, but across a long bridge or railway line it adds up to several centimetres, and engineers must allow for it with carefully placed gaps. Neglect those gaps, and a single hot summer afternoon can bend solid steel out of shape.

Heat can creep through a solid by conduction, in which quickly vibrating particles jostle their neighbours and pass the energy along like a whispered message. Metals are excellent conductors, because they have free electrons that carry energy swiftly, which is why the handle of a metal spoon in hot soup soon becomes uncomfortable. Wood and plastic conduct poorly, and that is why saucepans have handles made of them.

Heated air expands and becomes lighter, so it rises from a radiator towards the ceiling, while the cooler air at the other side of the room sinks to take its place. The result is a slow circulation that carries heat through the whole room, and the same process stirs a pan of water on a hob and drives the winds of the Earth. Convection is, in essence, heat travelling by hitching a ride on the moving matter that carries it.

Hold your hands towards a campfire and you feel the warmth immediately, even though the air between you and the flames may be cold and barely moving. Radiation carries heat as waves of light, mostly of a kind we cannot see, and these waves need no material to travel through. It is the only way for the Sun's warmth to cross about one hundred and fifty million kilometres of empty space and reach us.

Insulation is the art of slowing heat down on its journey from warm to cold. A woollen jumper holds a layer of still air, which is a poor conductor, and a vacuum flask goes further by leaving almost nothing at all between its double walls, with a shiny coating to reflect the radiation. The best way to keep something hot is to make it very hard for the heat to leave.

A cup of coffee left on a table cools until it matches the temperature of the room, and in all of human history no cup has ever warmed itself spontaneously by borrowing heat from the cooler air. Heat flows from hot to cold, and the exchange ends only when the temperatures are equal. Nothing in the rules of motion forbids the reverse, so this one-way street needs a deeper explanation.

Pour a jug of hot water into a bowl of cold water and the two soon blend into one pleasantly warm mixture, after which no amount of waiting will separate them again. The particles could in principle sort themselves into fast and slow groups, but the number of ways to be mixed is so vastly greater than the number of ways to be sorted that the mixed state wins every time. The one-way street of heat is therefore not a law of motion but simply a matter of overwhelming odds.

Imagine a pack of cards in perfect order and then the same pack shuffled thoroughly; the second arrangement is not special, but it is enormously more common than the first. Physicists measure how spread out energy has become with a quantity called entropy, which in an isolated system tends to increase simply because disorder can occur in so many more ways. This steady drift towards the more probable arrangement is the content of the famous second law of thermodynamics.

The steam engine burns fuel to boil water, and the expanding steam pushes a piston back and forth, turning the heat of a fire into useful motion. It drove the pumps, factories, ships and locomotives of the Industrial Revolution, and it also posed a puzzle that gave birth to the science of heat. Engineers wanted to know how much work could be wrung from a given amount of coal.

A heat engine works by letting heat flow from something hot to something cooler, and it can take work out of that flow, but never all of it. Some energy must always be thrown away to the cold side, which is why the engine of a typical petrol car wastes most of the energy in its fuel as warmth. This is not a flaw of design but a consequence of entropy that no clever engineer can escape.

For centuries inventors have dreamed of a machine that would run for ever without fuel, and many have built beautiful wheels, weights and magnets in the attempt. None has ever worked, because such a machine would have to create energy from nothing, or else reverse the spreading of heat, and nature allows neither. The failure of all those clever designs is among the best-established facts in science.

A refrigerator does not create cold so much as carry heat from the cool interior to the warmer kitchen, a journey that heat would never make by itself. It can do so only by spending electrical energy, and the warmth you feel at the back of the machine is the heat it has pumped out plus the energy it used. Heat can be made to flow uphill, but the bill must always be paid.

If you filmed a dropped egg and played the film backwards, you would know at once that something was wrong, since broken eggs never reassemble themselves. The basic laws of motion work perfectly well in either direction, so it is the tendency of entropy to rise that gives us a sense of before and after. Many physicists regard this as the best explanation we have for why time seems to flow in one direction.

Living things build intricate order from simple ingredients, which might seem to defy the rise of entropy, but the Earth is not an isolated system. Sunlight pours in, plants capture some of it, animals eat the plants, and in the end the energy leaves as heat radiated back into space, so the total disorder still increases. Life is therefore not an exception to the second law but a graceful way of riding along with it.

A pebble dropped into a still pond sends a ring of ripples racing outwards, yet a leaf floating nearby merely bobs up and down on the spot. A wave is a disturbance that travels, carrying energy from one place to another without carrying the material through which it passes. This simple fact is the key to sound, light, radio and a great deal more besides.

Every regular wave has crests and troughs, and two numbers describe it: the wavelength, the distance between neighbouring crests, and the frequency, the number of crests passing each second. Frequency is measured in hertz, in honour of the German physicist Heinrich Hertz, so a wave of ten hertz passes ten crests every second. Long waves have low frequencies and short waves have high ones, a pattern we will meet again with light.

Flick a rope and the wave runs along it while the rope itself moves from side to side, but squeeze a stretched spring and a pulse of crowded coils travels down its length instead. The first is a sideways wave and the second a squeezing wave, and nature uses both: light and water ripples are of the sideways kind, while sound is of the squeezing kind. Both kinds carry energy from place to place without carrying any of the matter that they pass through.

A plucked guitar string vibrates hundreds of times a second, shoving the neighbouring air first one way and then the other. Those shoves become a travelling wave of slightly squeezed and slightly stretched air, which spreads out from the instrument until it reaches an eardrum and makes it tremble in just the same pattern. You can feel the beginning of the whole process by resting a fingertip lightly on a string that is sounding.

A famous experiment places a ringing bell in a glass jar and then pumps the air out, and as the air thins the sound fades until the bell, though still clearly shaking, can scarcely be heard. Sound is a wave in matter and cannot cross a vacuum, which is why the explosions in films about space would, in reality, be perfectly silent. Light, by contrast, needs no such medium, and that difference will be important later.

Sound moves through air at about three hundred and forty metres every second, a speed that sounds impressive until it is compared with light, which is nearly a million times faster. Lightning and thunder are produced at the same moment, but the flash reaches you almost instantly while the rumble dawdles behind, and every three seconds of delay means roughly one kilometre of distance. Counting the gap is an old and surprisingly reliable way to judge a storm.

The pitch of a note depends on the frequency of its vibration: short, thin, tightly stretched strings quiver rapidly and sound high, while long, thick, loose ones sway slowly and sound deep. Loudness is a separate matter altogether, for it depends on how much energy the wave carries, so a big drum can sound far louder than a small whistle without being any higher. The whole of music, from a lullaby to a symphony, is built on these two independent dials.

A loud shout across a valley strikes the far cliff and returns a moment later as an echo, and the delay tells you how far away the cliff is. Bats and dolphins have perfected this trick, producing high squeaks and building a picture of the world from the replies, while ships use sonar to measure the depth of the sea below them. Echoes, in short, turn sound into a way of seeing in the dark, and nature discovered it long before we did.

As an ambulance rushes past, its siren seems to slide suddenly from a high note to a lower one, though the driver hears no change at all. In front of the moving vehicle the sound waves are crowded together, and behind it they are stretched out, so the listener meets them at a different rate on the way in than on the way out. This Doppler effect, named for an Austrian physicist, also lets police radar measure the speed of a car.

Everything that can swing or shake has a natural frequency at which it prefers to move, and gentle pushes timed to match it can build up a surprisingly large motion. A child on a swing knows this instinctively, and so does a singer who, in theory, can shatter a delicate glass with a loud note of exactly the right pitch. Resonance explains the tuning of a radio, the sound of a violin and the swaying of tall buildings.

Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second, a speed so great that it could circle the Earth more than seven times in a single second. Sunlight, which has to cross about a hundred and fifty million kilometres, reaches us in a little over eight minutes. When you look at the Sun, you are always seeing it as it was a short while ago.

Light travels in straight lines, and that is why a solid object blocks it so cleanly and casts a shadow whose outline matches its own. A sundial turns this fact into a clock, since the shadow of its pointer sweeps across the dial as the Sun moves through the sky. Ancient astronomers also used shadows to measure the heights of buildings and even the size of the Earth.

Distances between the stars are so enormous that astronomers measure them by the time light takes to cross them, and one light-year is about nine and a half million million kilometres. The nearest star beyond the Sun is a little over four light-years away, so the glimmer reaching your eye tonight set out more than four years ago. Looking up at the night sky is therefore a kind of time travel, and every glimmer shows the past.

A mirror reflects light according to a precise rule: the angle at which a ray leaves the surface is exactly equal to the angle at which it arrived. Because the surface is so smooth, all of the rays are returned in an orderly fashion and your eye sees a sharp image, whereas rough paper scatters them in every direction and shows nothing. Reflection is the reason we can see most objects at all, since they bounce light into our eyes.

Around 1666 Newton darkened a room, let a thin beam of sunlight fall on a glass prism and watched a band of colours spread across the wall. By sending that coloured light through a second prism he showed that the colours could be joined back into white, so the prism had not made the colours but had merely separated the ones already there. White light, he concluded, is a mixture, and that discovery was a landmark in the study of colour.

A rainbow appears when sunlight enters millions of raindrops, reflects from the inside of each one and emerges bent, with every colour turned through a slightly different angle. To see it, you must have the Sun behind you and the rain in front, and each person sees a bow that belongs to them alone, made by different drops from everyone else's. A rainbow is not an object in the sky but a pattern that depends on where you stand.

The colour of an everyday object is not painted on it but is the part of the light that it chooses to reflect. An apple looks red because it sends red light to your eyes and absorbs the rest, a leaf looks green for a similar reason, and a black cat looks black because it absorbs nearly everything that falls on it. In a room lit by pure green light, a red apple would look almost black.

Light slows down when it passes from air into water or glass, and when it enters at an angle, that slowing makes it change direction, a process called refraction. This is why a spoon seems to snap at the surface of a glass of water and why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is. The bending of light is not a trick but a rule, and glass can be shaped to exploit it.

A lens is a carefully curved piece of glass or other clear material that bends all the rays passing through it towards a single point. The lens inside your eye does exactly this, focusing the scene onto the retina at the back, and spectacles simply give it some help when it cannot do the job alone. A few simple pieces of glass have allowed millions of people to read and work in comfort.

Two lenses, arranged one way, make distant objects seem close, and arranged another way, make tiny ones seem large, which is the whole principle of the telescope and the microscope. In 1610 Galileo turned a telescope on Jupiter and saw four small moons circling it, evidence that not everything in the sky revolved around the Earth. The microscope, in the same century, revealed a hidden world of living things too small for any unaided eye.

Rub a balloon on your hair and tiny charges move from one surface to the other, leaving the balloon with a surplus and the hair with a shortage. The two now attract each other, which is why strands of hair rise to meet the balloon and why it will cling to a wall. This ancient curiosity, once only a parlour trick, turned out to be a window onto the force that holds the world together.

Nature supplies exactly two kinds of electric charge, which Benjamin Franklin labelled positive and negative, and the rule that governs them is beautifully simple. Charges that differ are drawn towards one another, while charges that match are driven apart, and the strength of the force weakens with distance. Almost everything around us, from the stiffness of a table to the glue between atoms, is a consequence of this one pattern.

Inside a thundercloud, countless ice crystals collide and charge builds up until the air can no longer hold it apart, and then it leaps to the ground in a brilliant spark. The air along the path is heated to a temperature several times hotter than the surface of the Sun, and its sudden expansion is what we hear as thunder. A metal lightning rod protects a building by offering the electricity an easy and harmless way down.

In a metal some of the electrons are not bound to any single atom, and they can drift through the material, carrying charge wherever it is needed. That makes metals excellent conductors, while plastic and rubber hold their electrons firmly in place and so insulate, which is why a copper wire is wrapped in a protective coat. Without this simple contrast between those who share and those who hoard, electrical engineering would hardly exist.

In the year 1800 the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta stacked discs of two different metals, separated by pieces of cloth soaked in salty water, and found that the pile produced a steady flow of electricity. Until then, electricity had been known only as a brief spark that vanished almost instantly, and the new device made it possible to study it patiently. Every battery in a phone or a torch today is a distant descendant of that humble pile.

An electric current is a flow of charge, and it can flow only if it has a complete loop to travel around, from the battery through the wire and the bulb and back again. Break the circuit anywhere, with a switch or a loose wire, and the flow stops everywhere at once, which is exactly how a light switch works. The charge does not get used up in the bulb, for it is the energy it carries that is spent.

A good picture for a circuit is water flowing between two tanks at different heights, where the height difference plays the part of voltage and the amount flowing each second plays the part of current. Voltage, measured in volts, is the push that the battery provides, and current, measured in amperes, tells you how much charge is actually moving. The comparison is not perfect, but it explains a great deal with very little effort.

Every material resists the flow of current to some degree, and a thin wire resists far more than a thick one, so the electrons lose energy as they struggle through. That lost energy appears as heat, and in the filament of an old bulb or the elements of a toaster the heat is intense enough to make the metal glow. Resistance is a nuisance in a power line, but an essential ingredient in a heater.

When components are joined end to end in a series circuit, the current has just one path to follow, so a single broken bulb halts the whole string, as many people have discovered with old festive lights. In a parallel circuit every device has its own branch, so one can fail or be switched off while the others carry on, and that is how the sockets in a home are wired. Choosing between the two arrangements is a basic skill of every electrician, and it is learned early in training.

If too much current flows through a wire, the wire heats up, and the result can be a fire, so every home circuit includes a safety device. A fuse contains a thin strip that melts and breaks the circuit when the current becomes excessive, and a circuit breaker does the same by switching itself off. Mains electricity can seriously hurt people, which is a good reason to leave all repairs to a trained electrician.

Magnets have been known since ancient times, when people noticed that a certain dark stone could pull small pieces of iron towards itself. Every magnet has two poles, called north and south, and they obey a rule much like the one for electric charge: like poles repel one another, while unlike poles attract. If you cut a magnet in half, you never get a lone pole, but two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south.

The influence of a magnet is not confined to its surface, since it fills the surrounding space with an invisible magnetic field. Scatter iron filings on a sheet of paper above a bar magnet and each tiny sliver becomes a small magnet itself, lining up along elegant curved lines that stretch from one pole to the other. Michael Faraday found this picture of invisible fields so useful that it became central to modern physics.

The needle of a compass is a light and delicate magnet, free to turn, and it swings round until it points along the magnetic field of the Earth. That simple behaviour reveals that our whole planet acts like an enormous magnet, with one pole near the north and another near the south, and sailors have relied on it for roughly a thousand years. Scientists believe that the field comes from swirling liquid iron deep inside the Earth.

The Sun continually blows out a stream of electrically charged particles, and the Earth's magnetic field deflects most of them away, funnelling a few towards the polar regions. When these particles strike the thin air high above the ground, they make it glow in shimmering curtains of green, red and violet that we call the aurora. The field is therefore more than a guide for travellers, since it is also a shield for life.

In 1820 the Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted was demonstrating electricity to students when he noticed a nearby compass needle twitch whenever a current flowed in a wire. The observation was startling, for it was the first evidence that electricity and magnetism, long regarded as unrelated, were two aspects of the same underlying thing. Within a few years the discovery had set off a chain of experiments that changed the world.

A wire carrying a current has a magnetic field around it, and if the wire is wound into a coil around an iron core, the effect becomes strong enough to lift a car. Its great advantage over an ordinary magnet is that it can be switched off, so a crane in a scrapyard can pick up a heap of metal and then release it exactly where it is wanted. Electromagnets also sit quietly inside doorbells, loudspeakers, electric motors and the large scanners used in hospitals.

A magnet exerts a force on a wire carrying a current, and if that wire is formed into a loop that can turn, the force makes the loop rotate. An electric motor arranges for the current to reverse at just the right moment, so that the push continues and the spinning never stops, converting electrical energy neatly into motion. Motors turn the fan on your desk, the wheels of a train and the drum of a washing machine.

If electricity can create magnetism, Michael Faraday reasoned, then magnetism ought to be able to create electricity, and in 1831 he proved that it could. When he pushed a magnet in and out of a coil of wire, a current flickered through the coil, though there was no battery anywhere in the circuit. The key, he found, was change: it is a changing magnetic field, and not a steady one, that pushes the charges along.

A generator is essentially Faraday's experiment made continuous, with a magnet spinning inside coils of wire so that a current is produced as long as the spinning goes on. The turning may be done by wind, by falling water or, in most power stations, by steam produced from burning fuel or from nuclear reactions. Nearly all the electricity that lights the world is therefore born from the motion of magnets past coils of wire.

Sending electricity along a wire wastes energy as heat, but the waste shrinks dramatically if the voltage is raised and the current lowered, which is why long power lines operate at tens or hundreds of thousands of volts. A transformer, which works because a changing current in one coil creates a current in another, steps the voltage up at the power station and down again near our homes. It is Faraday's discovery put to work on the scale of a whole country.

In the 1860s the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell gathered everything then known about electricity and magnetism into a short set of elegant equations. To his astonishment they predicted waves of electric and magnetic fields, moving through empty space at a speed that matched the measured speed of light. He drew the daring conclusion that light itself must be exactly such a wave, travelling through the world unseen.

In 1887 the German physicist Heinrich Hertz generated electric sparks in one part of his laboratory and detected the waves they produced in a loop of wire across the room. The waves reflected, bent and travelled at the speed of light, just as Maxwell's theory had foretold, and the doubters were silenced. Hertz himself saw no practical use for his discovery, yet within a few years it was carrying messages across oceans.

Visible light turns out to be only one narrow band in a vast family of electromagnetic waves, all of which travel at the same speed in empty space. What distinguishes a radio wave from an X-ray is merely its wavelength, which may be longer than a building or shorter than an atom. Nature, it seems, has been broadcasting on many channels all along, and our eyes happen to be tuned to just one.

Radio waves are the longest members of the family, with wavelengths that stretch from a few centimetres to many kilometres, and they pass through walls and clouds with ease. By varying a wave in a pattern that a receiver can decode, we can carry music, pictures or a whole telephone call through the air from one place to another. Your phone is at this very moment bathed in countless such invisible messages, and it picks out only the one meant for you.

A microwave oven fills its small metal box with waves of just the right length to be absorbed by the water in food, making the water molecules rotate vigorously and so generating heat. The dish itself stays comparatively cool, which is why a plate can sometimes feel less hot than the soup it holds. The same waves, used at lower power, carry signals between satellites, radar stations and mobile phones.

Everything that is warm glows, but its light lies in the infrared, a band of wavelengths just longer than red that our eyes cannot detect and our skin feels as warmth. The astronomer William Herschel found it in 1800 when a thermometer placed beyond the red end of a prism's spectrum began to warm up. Modern thermal cameras use this radiation to reveal people, animals and escaping heat in complete darkness.

The light that our eyes can detect is a minute portion of the electromagnetic family, with wavelengths ranging from about four hundred billionths of a metre for violet to seven hundred for red. It is no coincidence that this is where the Sun delivers most of its energy, since eyes that evolved on this planet were bound to exploit the light that was most abundant. The whole of human art and vision lives within one slender strip of the spectrum.

Just beyond the violet end of the spectrum lies ultraviolet light, which carries enough energy to damage living cells and burn the skin of the careless sunbather. A high layer of ozone in the atmosphere absorbs most of the harmful part before it reaches us, and sun cream and clothing do the rest, but many insects, including bees, can see ultraviolet and use it to find flowers. A colour that is quite invisible to us is, to them, a bright signpost pointing the way to food.

X-rays are electromagnetic waves so short and energetic that they pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser bone, so a photograph made with them shows a ghostly picture of the skeleton. They were discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895, and within months doctors were using them to find broken bones. Because large doses are harmful, modern medical X-rays use the smallest amounts that will do the job.

At the far end of the family are gamma rays, the shortest waves of all, produced by radioactive nuclei and by some of the most violent events in the universe, such as exploding stars. Their energy is so great that they can damage living cells, which makes them hazardous, yet carefully controlled beams are used to sterilise equipment and to target tumours in hospitals. One continuous family of waves thus runs from the radio in a kitchen to the flash of a dying star.

Everything you can touch, from the table to the air to your own hand, is built from atoms, and each atom is far smaller than anything a microscope of the old kind could show. Hundreds of thousands of them would fit side by side across the width of a single human hair. It is a sobering thought that a speck of dust contains more atoms than there are people on Earth.

More than two thousand years ago the Greek thinker Democritus wondered what would happen if you kept cutting a stone in half, and he guessed that there must be a smallest piece that could not be divided further. He called it an atom, a word that means uncuttable, but he had no experiments with which to test the guess. It would take more than two thousand years, and a great deal of ingenuity, for real evidence to arrive.

In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown noticed that specks of pollen floating in water jiggled constantly and unpredictably, and nobody could say why. In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that the specks were being knocked about by unseen water molecules, and he calculated how large the effect should be, which allowed experimenters to check it. After that, even the most stubborn sceptics of the time agreed that atoms were real and could be counted.

Surprisingly few kinds of atom are needed to build the whole natural world: about ninety, ranging from hydrogen, the lightest, to uranium, the heaviest of those found in nature. Each kind is called an element, and each has its own place in the periodic table, the famous chart in which the elements are arranged by weight and by chemical behaviour. Everything from a diamond to a daffodil is some combination of those ninety ingredients.

In 1897 the English physicist Joseph John Thomson studied a beam that glowed inside an almost empty glass tube and showed that it was a stream of particles far lighter than the lightest atom. He had discovered the electron, the first known piece of an atom, and the name atom, meaning uncuttable, was suddenly out of date. The thing that was supposed to be indivisible, it turned out, could be divided after all, and a new science began.

Around 1909 Ernest Rutherford's laboratory fired fast particles at a sheet of gold foil, expecting them to pass straight through, which most of them did. A very few, however, bounced almost straight back, and Rutherford later said it was as if a shell fired at tissue paper had come back at him. The only explanation was that nearly all of the atom's mass is crammed into a minute and dense nucleus at its centre.

Rutherford's picture of the atom is strange, for almost all of its volume is empty. If its nucleus were enlarged to the size of a pea at the centre of a great stadium, the electrons would be tiny specks circling the outermost seats, and everything between would be nothing at all. The solid feel of a table is therefore an illusion, produced by electric forces that stop one atom from sinking into another.

The electrons on the outside of an atom decide how it behaves with others, which means that the whole of chemistry is, in a sense, the study of electron sharing and swapping. When atoms join by this means they form molecules, and the molecule of water, with two atoms of hydrogen and one of oxygen, is the most familiar of them all. A few dozen rules about electrons thus explain the variety of everything from soap to stone.

The nuclei of some atoms are unstable and can break apart on their own, releasing energy in a process discovered by Henri Becquerel and studied by Marie and Pierre Curie. No one can say when a given nucleus will go, but the time it takes for half of a large sample to decay, called the half-life, is perfectly regular and can be measured. That steady clock lets scientists date ancient rocks and the remains of living things.

The Sun shines by fusion, in which the intense heat and pressure in its core force hydrogen nuclei together to make helium and release a torrent of energy. Nuclear power stations on Earth rely on the opposite process, fission, which splits the nuclei of heavy atoms such as uranium. Both exploit the fact that the nucleus holds far more energy than any chemical reaction can reach.

Maxwell's equations gave a single speed for light, without saying who was supposed to be measuring it, and that omission puzzled the physicists of the nineteenth century. In the 1880s the American scientists Albert Michelson and Edward Morley searched with great care for a change in that speed caused by the Earth's motion through space, and they found none at all. The riddle stood unresolved for almost twenty years, until a young man with no great reputation took it seriously.

In 1905 a young man named Albert Einstein was working as a clerk in the patent office in Bern, examining other people's inventions during the day. In his spare time he published several papers, any one of which would have made a career, and one of them proposed the theory we now call special relativity. It is difficult to think of another year in which a single mind changed so much so quickly.

Einstein's response to the puzzle was to accept it at face value and to follow the consequences wherever they might lead. Whoever measures the speed of light gets exactly the same result, however fast that observer is travelling, so a person chasing a light beam would still see it recede at full speed. It is a claim that defies everyday intuition, and yet experiments have confirmed it again and again.

If light has the same speed for everybody, then something else has to give, and Einstein showed that what gives is time. A clock on a fast train ticks more slowly as seen from the platform, and a platform clock seems slow to the traveller on the train. The effect is real, but at everyday speeds it is far too small to notice.

Picture a clock whose tick is the journey of a pulse of light between two mirrors, one above the other. When the clock is carried sideways, a watcher sees the pulse follow a longer, slanting path, yet because the speed of light cannot change, the extra distance can only be accounted for by a longer time between ticks. This elegant argument shows that slow time is not a flaw in clocks but a feature of time itself.

The theory has been tested repeatedly, and in 1971 scientists carried exact atomic clocks around the world in airliners and compared them afterwards with clocks that had stayed at home. The differences, a matter of billionths of a second, agreed with the predictions of relativity. In the upper atmosphere, short-lived particles called muons survive far longer than expected when they rush towards the ground at almost the speed of light, a spectacular confirmation of the same idea.

Light's speed turns out to be a cosmic limit that nothing with mass can ever reach, let alone exceed. As an object speeds up, every further increase demands more and more energy, and the supply required to bring it all the way to the speed of light would be infinite. Only light itself, which has no mass, travels at that speed, and it has never been able to go any slower in empty space.

Another startling consequence of relativity is that two events which seem simultaneous to one observer may happen at different moments for another who is moving relative to the first. Neither is mistaken, since each is describing the same events faithfully from a different point of view, and there is no single universal present that everyone must share. The comfortable idea of a common now is a useful approximation that works only at low speeds.

Perhaps the most famous result of Einstein's 1905 work is that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, linked by the equation E equals m c squared. Because the speed of light is so large, and is multiplied by itself, even a tiny amount of matter corresponds to an enormous quantity of energy, enough in principle for a pebble to power a city for a while. Most of that energy is locked away and cannot be released by any ordinary means.

Deep in its core the Sun converts about four million tonnes of matter into energy every second, which is the clearest everyday proof that mass and energy are interchangeable. This sounds like a staggering loss, yet the Sun is so enormous that it has shed only a minute fraction of its mass during the billions of years it has been shining. Every ray of sunlight that warms your face is a tiny piece of the Sun that has turned into light.

Special relativity said that nothing can travel faster than light, but Newton's gravity acted across space instantly, and the two ideas could not be reconciled. Einstein spent about ten difficult years searching for a new theory of gravity that would respect the cosmic speed limit, and he completed it in 1915. He called it general relativity, and it is among the most beautiful achievements of human thought.

Einstein later called it the happiest thought of his life: a person falling freely in a closed lift would feel no weight at all, and a ball released in front of him would simply hang in the air. From inside, there would be no way to tell a free fall near a planet from floating in empty space, and no way to tell standing on a planet from being accelerated upwards. That equivalence between falling and floating became the seed from which the whole of general relativity grew.

In Einstein's theory, gravity is not a force reaching across space but a feature of the shape of space and time themselves. A massive object such as the Sun bends the space around it, much as a heavy ball sinks into a stretched rubber sheet, and a passing planet simply follows the straightest path available on that curved surface. The Earth moves round the Sun not because it is pulled, but because it is following the bend.

Relativity does not treat space and time as separate stages but as a single four-part fabric called spacetime, with three directions of space and one of time. The American physicist John Wheeler summed up the theory in a famous phrase: matter tells spacetime how to curve, and curved spacetime tells matter how to move. Gravity, in this picture, is not a mysterious pull at all, but simply geometry in action on a cosmic scale.

In 1919 the English astronomer Arthur Eddington took expeditions to photograph stars close to the Sun during a total eclipse, when the sky grew dark enough to see them. The positions of the stars had shifted by just the amount that Einstein's theory predicted, because their light had been bent on its way past the Sun. Newspapers around the world announced the result, and a quiet clerk-turned-professor became a celebrity overnight.

General relativity predicts that time passes a little more slowly where gravity is stronger, so a clock at the foot of a tower ticks marginally slower than one at the top. The difference is almost unimaginably small, but atomic clocks are now so precise that it can be measured even across a height of a few tens of centimetres. You age very slightly less quickly on the ground floor of a building than on the top one.

The satellites that make up the global positioning system carry atomic clocks, and the signals from them are timed to a few billionths of a second. Their clocks run faster because of weaker gravity and slower because of their speed, and engineers must correct for both effects, or position errors would grow by several kilometres every day. A familiar map on a phone depends, quietly, on the theories of Albert Einstein.

A black hole is a region of spacetime so sharply curved that nothing, not even light, can escape once it has crossed the boundary known as the event horizon. Such objects form when a very massive star exhausts its fuel and collapses under its own weight, and there are millions of them in our galaxy alone. Despite the popular image, a black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner, and it attracts objects no more strongly than any other mass at the same distance.

In 2019 a network of radio telescopes spread across the planet, called the Event Horizon Telescope, produced the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the heart of the galaxy known as Messier 87. A ring of glowing gas surrounded a dark centre, just as Einstein's equations suggested, and in 2022 the same team published an image of the black hole at the centre of our own Milky Way. Something that had once been purely theoretical, a prediction on paper, had at last become something that could be photographed.

In September 2015 the two detectors of the LIGO experiment in the United States registered a faint shiver of spacetime, a gravitational wave that had been travelling for more than a billion years since two black holes merged. The stretching it produced was about a thousand times smaller than the width of a proton, and measuring it was one of the most delicate feats in the history of science. Einstein had predicted such waves a century earlier, and had doubted that anyone could ever detect them.

A poker heated in a furnace glows dull red, then orange, then a dazzling yellow-white, and by 1900 the pattern of that glow had stubbornly refused to fit any theory. The German physicist Max Planck rescued the situation with a desperate guess, that energy is given out and taken in only in small separate packets, and he reluctantly found that the guess worked perfectly. He had, without quite meaning to, started the quantum revolution, and the old certainties would not survive it.

When light falls on a clean metal surface it can knock electrons out of it, but the details of the effect baffled physicists, since brighter light did not make the electrons any faster. In 1905 Einstein proposed that light itself arrives in separate packets of energy, later named photons, and that each photon can eject only a single electron. For this work, and not for relativity, he received the Nobel Prize in 1921, a fact that surprises many people today.

Inside an atom an electron cannot have just any energy but only certain particular values, rather as a person can stand on the rungs of a ladder but not between them. When the electron drops to a lower rung it emits a photon of one exact colour, so each element has a unique pattern of coloured lines, like a fingerprint. By studying those lines in starlight, astronomers have learned what distant stars are made of.

On a smooth slope a ball can come to rest at any height at all, whereas on a staircase it can rest only on the steps, and quantum theory discovered that much of nature resembles the staircase. Energies, in atoms and in light, are not infinitely adjustable but come in distinct portions, which the German word quanta describes, and a quantum is simply one such portion. This simple departure from smoothness turned out to explain the behaviour of every atom.

Shine a beam of light through two narrow slits and the screen behind them does not show two bright bands but a whole series of fine stripes, bright and dark in turn. The explanation is that waves emerging from the two slits overlap, reinforcing one another in some places and cancelling in others, a behaviour unique to waves. The experiment was carried out in 1801 by Thomas Young, and it persuaded most scientists that light is a wave.

When electrons are fired through two slits one at a time, each arrives at the screen as a single tiny dot, just as a particle should. Yet as thousands of dots accumulate, they form the striped pattern of interfering waves, as though every individual electron had somehow explored both routes at once. Light and matter appear to behave sometimes as particles and sometimes as waves, and neither picture alone is complete.

In 1927 the German physicist Werner Heisenberg showed that certain pairs of properties, such as the position and the momentum of a particle, can never both be known with perfect precision. The more exactly one is pinned down, the more vague the other becomes, and this uncertainty is not caused by clumsy instruments but is built into the way nature works. The old picture of tiny billiard balls with definite paths had to be abandoned.

Quantum theory can predict with astonishing accuracy how many atoms in a large sample will decay in a given time, yet it cannot say when any single atom will do so. It deals in probabilities, and physicists still argue about whether this reflects something deep about reality or merely the limits of what we can know. The calculations are agreed by everyone, while the meaning of the calculations remains an open and lively debate.

In 1935 the Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger described an imaginary cat sealed in a box with a mechanism triggered by the decay of a single atom, and he asked what a quantum description of the box could possibly mean. He intended it as a way of exposing how strange it sounds to apply the rules of the very small to ordinary life, and not as a recipe for any real experiment. Physicists still disagree about what actually happens when a measurement is made, and the debate is far from settled.

However remote the quantum world may feel, its rules are the foundation of lasers, of the transistors in every computer chip, and of the atomic clocks that keep time for the whole planet. They underlie medical scanners, solar panels and the glow of an energy-saving lamp, and engineers are now trying to build quantum computers that exploit the strangeness itself. The theory that astonished its own inventors has become one of the most useful ever devised.

Beneath the farmland near Geneva runs a ring-shaped tunnel about twenty-seven kilometres around, which holds the Large Hadron Collider, the largest machine ever built. Beams of protons are driven round it at almost the speed of light and made to collide, and the debris is recorded by detectors the size of cathedrals. Such experiments have shown that protons and neutrons are not the end of the story, since each is built from three smaller particles called quarks.

The Standard Model is the physicists' catalogue of the basic ingredients of matter, and it has been tested to extraordinary precision. It contains six kinds of quark, six lighter particles including the electron, and a handful of carriers of force, of which the photon, the particle of light, is the most familiar. Everything in the ordinary world, from a daffodil to a star, is built from just a few of them.

All the pushes and pulls of the world, it appears, come down to just four basic forces. Gravity shapes the cosmos and electromagnetism governs atoms, chemistry and light, while two forces acting only inside the nucleus complete the set: the strong force, which glues quarks together, and the weak force, behind some radioactivity. Whether these four are really aspects of one deeper force is still an open question.

In 2012 two teams of scientists at CERN announced the discovery of the Higgs particle, almost fifty years after several theorists had predicted that it must exist. The particle is a ripple in a field that fills all of space and gives mass to many of the other basic particles, which would otherwise fly about at the speed of light. It was a triumph for a theory that had been written down on paper long before a machine existed that could test it.

For each basic particle there exists an antiparticle with the same mass but the opposite charge, a possibility first suggested by the British physicist Paul Dirac and confirmed when the positron was found in 1932. When a particle meets its antiparticle the pair annihilate, turning entirely into energy, and a hospital scanner called a PET scanner puts that fact to work in medicine. Why the universe contains so much matter and so little antimatter remains an unsolved mystery.

The Sun is only one of several hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, a spiral of light so large that it takes light about a hundred thousand years to cross it. Telescopes reveal that our galaxy is itself a single member of a population of hundreds of billions of galaxies, scattered through space in clusters and chains. Our place in the cosmos is a small one, and yet we are the part of it that has learned to ask questions.

In the 1920s astronomers, notably Edwin Hubble, measured the light of distant galaxies and found it systematically stretched towards the red, the signature of motion away from us. The farther away a galaxy lies, the faster it recedes, and the explanation is not that galaxies are racing through space but that space itself is expanding.
