Wherever an observer might stand, the other galaxies would appear to be moving away.

If the galaxies are now moving apart, then in the past they must have been closer, and following the argument back leads to a hot, dense beginning close to fourteen billion years ago. The faint afterglow of that early heat, now cooled into weak microwaves that fill the whole sky, was discovered in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who at first suspected that their antenna was dirty. It is the oldest light that we can see, a photograph of the universe as it was when it was very young.

Stars near the rim of a spiral galaxy orbit much faster than the visible matter could possibly allow, a fact documented in the 1970s by the American astronomer Vera Rubin. The simplest explanation is a halo of unseen dark matter, which pulls on the stars with gravity but neither shines nor absorbs light, yet no one has so far detected a single particle of it directly. Most of the matter in the universe is therefore a substance we know only by its pull.

Careful measurements suggest that ordinary matter, the stuff of stars, planets and people, makes up only about five percent of the universe, with roughly a quarter being dark matter. The remainder is called dark energy, a name for whatever is causing the expansion of the universe to speed up, as discovered by studies of exploding stars in 1998. Dark matter and dark energy are therefore labels for puzzles, and not explanations, which is exactly why they excite scientists so much.

What gives physics its power is not cleverness but testing, since a good theory must make a prediction that an experiment could, in principle, prove wrong. Ideas that fail are discarded without sentiment, and those that survive test after test earn our trust, though never absolute certainty. A theory that could explain anything, whatever happened, would in fact explain nothing at all, and so could never be tested.

By the 1840s the orbit of Uranus was drifting away from the path that Newton's laws predicted, and the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier suspected a hidden planet pulling on it. In 1846 he calculated where such a planet should lie, and the astronomer Johann Galle found Neptune within about one degree of the spot that very night. It was a spectacular victory for the idea that the same laws govern the whole of the heavens.

The orbit of Mercury slowly turns in space by a tiny amount each century that Newton's laws could not account for, and some astronomers, remembering Neptune, proposed another hidden planet. No such world was ever found, and in 1915 Einstein showed that his new theory of gravity explained the drift exactly. The same method that succeeded with Neptune thus failed with Mercury, and in the second case it was the theory that needed replacing.

In 2011 a team of physicists in Italy announced a startling result: particles called neutrinos seemed to have travelled slightly faster than light, in apparent violation of relativity. The scientists themselves were cautious, invited others to look for mistakes and eventually traced the effect to a loose cable in their equipment, so that the corrected measurement agreed with Einstein after all. The episode showed science at its best, which lies not in never making mistakes but in finding and correcting them.

No discovery is accepted merely because one person reports it, for a result must be reproduced by independent teams using different equipment before it is believed. Physicists also set a demanding standard of evidence, insisting that the chance of the observed signal being a statistical accident be extremely small, which is why the Higgs announcement waited until two experiments agreed. Scepticism is not an obstacle to science but its main safeguard, and every great result has passed through it.

General relativity governs the large, the heavy and the fast, while quantum theory governs the small, and each has passed every test that has been set for it. The trouble is that they are built on incompatible ideas, and nobody has yet found a single theory of gravity that respects both. The two collide at exactly the places we most want to understand, the centre of a black hole and the first moment of the universe.

Physicists have proposed several ambitious ways to unite gravity with quantum theory, among them string theory, in which particles are tiny vibrating loops, and a rival approach called loop quantum gravity. They are mathematically elegant and have taught us a great deal, but at present none makes a prediction that we can test and none has been confirmed by any experiment. Until nature says yes, they remain promising conjectures and not established science, however beautiful the mathematics may be.

For all that it has achieved, physics has left great questions unanswered: what dark matter and dark energy are, why matter outweighs antimatter, and what, if anything, came before the first moment. Some of these puzzles may be solved within a few decades, while others may take centuries or may require ideas that nobody has had yet. A science with no open questions would be a finished one, and physics is nowhere near finished.

The ideas we have met are not confined to laboratories, but are at work in the most ordinary of days. Behind the kettle's heat, the cable's current, the phone's chip and the satellite that finds you on a map stand a few principles, patiently tested and put to use. To understand them is to see the same world, but with its machinery showing.

We began with a thrown ball and a cooling cup, and we have travelled by way of waves, atoms and bent space to the edge of what is known. The remarkable thing is how few ideas were needed to cover so much ground, and how well each of them has been tested. Physics has not run out of questions, and some of the best ones may be waiting for the next person who looks at an ordinary thing and asks why.
